_comment: Generated by build/nodes.py from dist/ess.json + api/nodes.overlay.json. Do not hand-edit; edit the overlay instead. Node type ids are prefixed essgen/ so they cannot collide with the visual editor's own hand-written ess/ nodes.

nodes.title: AI Orders: Command
nodes.desc: Gives a group of spawned units an order - move, patrol, defend, attack, follow and so on. This is the node most likely to look like it did nothing, and the cause is almost always the options: each behavior needs its own fields, and a move with no destination is thrown away entirely. Orders are forced through, so a fresh order overrides a hold or defend the units were locked into (without that, units coming off a guard order just keep standing there). An order aimed at a vehicle is handed to its driver for you. Walking destinations work by quietly spawning an invisible marker prop at the spot and sending the units to THAT - a bare coordinate is silently ignored by anyone on foot - so pass a tracker if you want those props cleaned up afterwards.
nodes.desc_short: Gives a group of spawned units an order - move, patrol, defend, attack, follow and so on.

params.name: guids
params.desc: The units to order, as a Lua list. Wire in what a spawn node handed you, or look up a group you filed with the AI Orders: Set Group node. A name that was never filed gives an EMPTY list, and an order to an empty list commands nobody with no error at all.

params.name: behavior
params.desc: One of: move, patrol, defend, attack, hold, face, follow, flee, enter, deploy, animate. What each looks like in play - move: walk to a spot and stop. patrol: walk a route of points over and over. defend: walk to a spot then hold that area and fight anything that comes inside it. attack: hunt a target down. hold: stand still where they are and never give chase. face: turn to look at a point without moving. follow: tag along like a recruited buddy, keeping pace and climbing in and out of vehicles on their own. flee: run away from the player. enter: climb into a vehicle. deploy: a transport disgorges its passengers. animate: play a canned action such as cowering. Any other word is logged and nothing happens.

params.name: opts
params.desc: The settings for the chosen behavior, and the usual reason nothing happens. move, face and defend need at = {x, y, z} - without it the order is dropped and the units carry on with whatever they were doing. patrol needs points = {{x,y,z},{x,y,z}} and walks it forever unless you add loop = false. defend takes radius (12). attack, follow and enter take target, which is either a group name you filed or a unit/vehicle handle - and with NO target both attack and follow fall back to the nearest hero, which means they turn on the PLAYER. flee takes distance (120). animate takes action ('Cower'). enter takes role ('passenger', 'driver' or 'gunner') and gets the vehicle unlocked for you, which a freshly spawned vehicle needs before anyone can board it. Most behaviors also accept speed, priority ('hi', 'med' or 'lo'), and onComplete for a move or a non-looping patrol.

params.name: tracker
params.desc: Optional. Hand it an Ess.Track and the invisible destination markers this spawns get removed when you tear the rest of your setup down. Leave it blank and they sit in the world for the rest of the session.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order ran without a Lua error. It is NOT a promise the units accepted it - an unknown behavior name gives false, but a move with no destination still reports true even though nothing was ordered. If your units stand still, read the log rather than this.

nodes.title: AI Orders: Get Group
nodes.desc: Looks up the units filed under a name by the AI Orders: Set Group node, so you can feed them into an order or count them.
nodes.desc_short: Looks up the units filed under a name by the AI Orders: Set Group node, so you can feed them into an order or...

params.name: name
params.desc: The name you filed the units under.

returns.name: guids
returns.desc: The list of unit handles. An unknown or misspelled name gives an EMPTY list rather than an error, which is the usual reason an order aimed at a group commands nobody.

nodes.title: AI Orders: Set Group
nodes.desc: Files a list of units under a name, so later orders can point at the whole group by that name - 'attack the CONVOY group' - instead of wiring the list all over your graph. It is purely a label store: nothing spawns, moves or changes in the world when you call it.
nodes.desc_short: Files a list of units under a name, so later orders can point at the whole group by that name - 'attack the...

params.name: name
params.desc: The name to file them under. Any word you like, but spell it the same way when you use it - an unknown name reads back as an empty group and orders aimed at it quietly do nothing.

params.name: guids
params.desc: The list of unit handles to file, as a Lua list. Normally wired straight from whatever spawned them.

nodes.title: Atmosphere: Blend In Progress
nodes.desc: Tells you whether the engine is part-way through taking the sky over right now. Crossing into an atmosphere region does not overwrite your look outright - it starts a blend, roughly a second long, from whatever you set toward that region's own settings. Check this before re-applying a change: applying during the blend just feeds fresh input to the thing that is overwriting you. BIG TRAP - do not use this in the same frame as any other Atmosphere node. Reading or setting a value opens a transaction, and the engine counts a transaction as a blend, so this reads true for the rest of that frame no matter what. Put it first in the chain, or read it on a later tick such as a loop heartbeat, which is where you would be waiting anyway.
nodes.desc_short: Tells you whether the engine is part-way through taking the sky over right now.

returns.name: blending
returns.desc: True while a region blend is running. Wait for it to go false before re-applying your look.

nodes.title: Atmosphere: Read Sky Value
nodes.desc: Reads one number out of the sky and lighting settings - how bright the light is, how strong the haze is, how much the picture glows. The engine only hands these numbers out inside an open transaction and quietly returns nothing outside one, which is why copying the game's own script for this gets you nothing; this node opens and closes that transaction for you. Second trap: names are never checked, so a misspelled one reads back 0 rather than failing, and since 0 is a real value for several settings you cannot use it to tell a typo from a genuine reading.
nodes.desc_short: Reads one number out of the sky and lighting settings - how bright the light is, how strong the haze is, how...

params.name: sKey
params.desc: Which value to read. Use one of the friendly names - lightIntensity, atmosphereForce, atmosphereLimit, timeRestore, bloomAmount, bloomMultiplier, bloomThreshold, bloomBlurRadius, bloomTargetLuminance, bloomContrastMultiplier, bloomContrastLimit, bloomAdaptiveLuminanceScale, bloomAdaptiveLuminancePct - or the raw engine name such as fLightIntensity. Prefer the friendly names: the engine misspells two of its own keys as fBloomContastMultiplier and fBloomContastLimit (Contast, not Contrast), so typing those correctly by hand silently does nothing forever.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: The current value of that setting, or nothing at all if the read failed. A flat 0 usually means the name was wrong rather than the value really being 0.

nodes.title: Atmosphere: Find Atmosphere Region
nodes.desc: Looks up one of the map's named atmosphere regions and gives you its handle. These are the zones responsible for your sky changes not sticking - there are forty of them across the map, each with its own authored look. Only six are named in the game's own scripts (rgn_atmo_caracas, rgn_atmo_Maracaibo, rgn_atmo_Angelfalls, rgn_atmo_interior, rgn_atmo_PMCinterior, rgn_atmo_carmonaislandrain), though many more exist in the level data. Honest note: nothing else in Ess accepts a region handle yet - this node exists so the work of reconfiguring what a region applies can start from something solid.
nodes.desc_short: Looks up one of the map's named atmosphere regions and gives you its handle.

params.name: sName
params.desc: The region's name, always starting with rgn_atmo_. Capitalisation does not matter - rgn_atmo_caracas and rgn_atmo_Caracas are the same region.

returns.name: region
returns.desc: A handle for that region, or nothing at all if no region goes by that name.

nodes.title: Atmosphere: Set Sky Values
nodes.desc: Changes one or several sky and lighting numbers at once, fading smoothly to the new look. Set them all in ONE node rather than several: the fade length belongs to the whole batch, so splitting a change across separate nodes gives you separate fades and a visibly staggered, ugly result. Be aware the change is not permanent - the map is carved into regions that each paint their own sky, and crossing into one starts a blend that carries your settings away over about a second.
nodes.desc_short: Changes one or several sky and lighting numbers at once, fading smoothly to the new look.

params.name: tKeyToValue
params.desc: A list of name-and-number pairs, written as { name = number, name = number }. Names are the friendly ones (lightIntensity, bloomAmount, atmosphereForce and so on) or raw engine names. Nothing checks them: an unknown name raises no error and reports no failure, it simply never does anything.

params.name: nFadeSeconds
params.desc: How many seconds the world takes to ease into the new look. 0 snaps instantly. Leave it empty for half a second.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True means the change went through - it does NOT mean your names were real. The engine never reports an unknown name, so a typo still reports success.

nodes.title: Atmosphere: Set Sky Colour
nodes.desc: Paints one of the atmosphere's colour slots - most usefully the ambient colour, the light that washes over everything and tints the whole world. Like the other atmosphere nodes it fades in and is then at the mercy of the region system: drive into a new atmosphere region and the engine blends your colour away toward that region's own look. The friendlier Easy World: Tint node does the same job and keeps re-applying itself so it survives crossings.
nodes.desc_short: Paints one of the atmosphere's colour slots - most usefully the ambient colour, the light that washes over...

params.name: sKey
params.desc: Which colour slot to paint. Use ambient for the big one that tints everything, rim for the edge light, or a raw engine name such as uiAmbientColor. There is also a set of six sky-box faces - name one directly (uiAmbientCube0 through uiAmbientCube5); the group name ambientCube is a list of six rather than one slot, so this node refuses it and does nothing.

params.name: r
params.desc: Red, 0 to 255. Left empty it is 255. For the deep red the game's hellscape look uses, try 220 here with 30 for green and blue.

params.name: g
params.desc: Green, 0 to 255. Left empty it is 255.

params.name: b
params.desc: Blue, 0 to 255. Left empty it is 255. All three at 255 is plain white, which is the neutral do-nothing colour.

params.name: a
params.desc: How strongly the colour applies, 0 to 255. Every real use of this in the game's own scripts leaves it at 255, so leave it alone unless you are experimenting.

params.name: nFadeSeconds
params.desc: How many seconds the colour takes to fade in. 0 snaps instantly. Leave it empty for half a second.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True means the change went through. It does not prove the slot name was real - a wrong name reports success and changes nothing.

nodes.title: Atmosphere: Set Time Of Day
nodes.desc: Moves the time-of-day clock, which really does turn the sky to night on screen. Two things will bite you. The clock keeps running from wherever you put it, so pair this with Atmosphere: Set Time Speed at 0 or it drifts straight back out again. And this does NOT hold across the whole map: the map has forty atmosphere regions, each painting its own sky directly rather than from the clock, so crossing into one blends your night away - measured live, a night sky faded back to full daylight over about a second at a boundary. If you want a time that holds as well as it can, use Easy World: Night or Easy World: Lock Time Of Day, which keep re-applying it.
nodes.desc_short: Moves the time-of-day clock, which really does turn the sky to night on screen.

params.name: n
params.desc: How far through the day, as a fraction from 0 to 1 rather than an hour. 0.95 reads as night, 0.30 as daytime.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the clock was moved. False only if you handed it something that was not a number.

nodes.title: Atmosphere: Set Time Speed
nodes.desc: Sets how fast the day/night cycle runs, with 0 freezing it completely. This is the RELIABLE half of time control: the rate is global state that region presets leave alone, so a freeze survives crossing region boundaries even with nothing re-applying it, where forcing a specific time of day does not. One-way trip, though - the engine can set the rate but offers no way to ask what it was, so once you change it the game's own pace cannot be restored short of reloading the level.
nodes.desc_short: Sets how fast the day/night cycle runs, with 0 freezing it completely.

params.name: n
params.desc: The speed of the cycle. 0 stops it dead - that is the setting you almost always want. Be careful with 1: it is not 'normal speed', it races a whole day past in a few seconds, so a natural-looking pace means a much smaller number found by trial.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the speed was applied. False only if you handed it something that was not a number.

nodes.title: Atmosphere: Active Setting Handle
nodes.desc: Hands back a marker for whichever atmosphere preset the world is using right now. The marker itself is not readable - its whole purpose is comparison. Store it, compare it against a fresh one a moment later, and when the two differ you have crossed into a region that just took the sky over, which is your cue to re-apply. One warning: never try to turn this marker into text. On this build turning two values into text at once gives you back a function, which is a very convincing way to fool yourself into thinking a stored marker has changed when it has not.
nodes.desc_short: Hands back a marker for whichever atmosphere preset the world is using right now.

returns.name: setting
returns.desc: A marker for the active atmosphere preset. Only useful compared against another one; the engine actually returns two of these and this gives you the first, which is the one that actually changes when you cross a region.

nodes.title: Bones: Aim Direction Between Two Hardpoints
nodes.desc: Works out which way a mounted part is pointing by taking the line from one hardpoint to another on the same model - a turret's breech to its barrel tip gives you the barrel line, confirmed live on the Allied Destroyer's cannon. Use it to put a muzzle effect in the right place, send something flying along the barrel, or aim a camera down the gun. Gives you nothing if either name doesn't exist on that model, and note that a freshly spawned model's hardpoints read as nothing for about a third of a second - wait for it first.
nodes.desc_short: Works out which way a mounted part is pointing by taking the line from one hardpoint to another on the same...

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The vehicle or character carrying both hardpoints. They must be on the SAME object.

params.name: hpBase
params.desc: Name of the hardpoint at the BACK of the part - where the line starts.

params.name: hpTip
params.desc: Name of the hardpoint at the FRONT - where the line ends. Base to tip is the direction the part is pointing.

returns.name: dx
returns.desc: East/west part of the direction. These three are a DIRECTION, not a place - add them onto the base hardpoint's position to travel along the barrel.

returns.name: dy
returns.desc: Up/down part of the direction - this is what tells you the barrel is raised or lowered.

returns.name: dz
returns.desc: North/south part of the direction.

nodes.promoted_from_getter: multi-value return cannot be spliced inline as an expression

nodes.title: Bones: Attach Effect To A Bone
nodes.desc: Glues a particle effect (smoke, fire, a glow) onto a named bone or hardpoint of a character or vehicle so it rides along as the model moves - a plume off someone's head, flames on an engine, a flash at a gun muzzle. Every bone on a person and every hardpoint on a vehicle is reachable by name, because the engine hashes the name rather than looking up text, so 'hp_' hardpoints and raw 'bone_' skeleton joints both work. TRAP: a model you have JUST spawned reports no bones for about a third of a second, so this quietly gives you nothing if you run it the instant you create something - put a Wait Until Model Is Ready node in front of it.
nodes.desc_short: Glues a particle effect (smoke, fire, a glow) onto a named bone or hardpoint of a character or vehicle so it...

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The character or vehicle to stick the effect to. Defaults to you, which is the easiest way to see that it worked.

params.name: bone
params.desc: The name of the bone or hardpoint to pin to. Bone_Head and Bone_Chest are confirmed human joints; vehicles use their own hp_ names like hp_barreltip_cannon. A name that doesn't exist isn't an error - you just get nothing back.

params.name: template
params.desc: The name of the effect to create. The default is a confirmed-working tall smoke plume. A blank name is refused on purpose - an empty name crashes the game outright, and that crash cannot be caught.

returns.name: uFx
returns.desc: The effect that was created. KEEP this - it is the only way to take the effect off again later, via the Detach Effect node. You get nothing back if the bone name didn't resolve, the name was blank, or the game refused to create it.

nodes.title: Bones: Detach Effect
nodes.desc: Takes an effect back off a bone and removes it from the world - the undo for Attach Effect To A Bone. Safe to run on nothing at all: that is a harmless do-nothing rather than an error, so you don't need to check first before cleaning up.
nodes.desc_short: Takes an effect back off a bone and removes it from the world - the undo for Attach Effect To A Bone.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The character or vehicle the effect was glued to.

params.name: uFx
params.desc: The effect to remove - wire in the one you got back from Attach Effect To A Bone. Left empty, nothing happens.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if an effect was actually removed. False just means there was nothing to remove.

nodes.title: Bones: Probe Bone Names
nodes.desc: A discovery tool for finding out what a model's bones are called. You give it a list of name beginnings and a list of endings; it tries every combination and reports which ones resolved to a real point, with the coordinates it found. HARD CAVEAT, keep it in mind: bone names are hashed, so a nonsense string can collide onto a real bone and hand back real, valid coordinates. A hit proves the string is a usable handle for SOME node on that model - it does NOT prove that node is really called that. Use this to explore, never as the foundation of a finished mod.
nodes.desc_short: A discovery tool for finding out what a model's bones are called.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The model to probe. The player character is the easiest thing to try it on.

params.name: prefixes
params.desc: A Lua list of name beginnings to try, each in quotes inside the braces.

params.name: suffixes
params.desc: A Lua list of name endings. Every beginning is joined to every ending, so 2 beginnings and 4 endings means 8 names tried.

returns.name: hits
returns.desc: The names that resolved - a list where each entry carries name, x, y and z as read at the moment of the probe.

returns.name: nTried
returns.desc: How many name combinations were tried in total (duplicates are only tried once), so you can see the hit rate.

nodes.promoted_from_getter: multi-value return cannot be spliced inline as an expression

nodes.title: Bones: Wait Until Model Is Ready
nodes.desc: The fix for the most common bone bug there is. A model you have just spawned reports no position and no bones for roughly a third of a second, so reading a bone the moment you create something silently does nothing and looks like your names are wrong. This checks ten times a second until the object's position can actually be read, then runs your code once. If the object never becomes readable it gives up after a set number of tries and runs your code anyway (writing a line to the log), so nothing can hang forever - your code should still check that the exact bone it wants exists.
nodes.desc_short: The fix for the most common bone bug there is.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The object to wait on - normally wired straight out of a Spawn node. The player character is already loaded, so with the default your code runs almost immediately.

params.name: cb
params.desc: Your code, run once the model is ready. It receives the object so you can act on it. If your code errors, the error is caught and written to the log instead of breaking anything else.

params.name: maxTries
params.desc: How many tenth-of-a-second checks before giving up and running your code regardless. 6 (about 0.6 seconds) is the default and comfortably clears the confirmed third-of-a-second window.

nodes.title: Camera: Begin Cinematic (Takes Control)
nodes.desc: TAKES OVER the player's camera and locks their look control away so you can frame a shot. Nothing from Place Camera, Look At or Hold shows up until this has run. You MUST give control back with End Cinematic - always build the way out at the same time as the way in. If you ever do get stuck with a frozen camera, the Panic Revert node always works and can be fired blind.
nodes.desc_short: TAKES OVER the player's camera and locks their look control away so you can frame a shot.

params.name: i
params.desc: Whose camera to take over. 0 is you; 1 is the co-op partner, which doesn't exist in single-player and simply fails.

params.name: nBlend
params.desc: Seconds to ease into the shot. 1 is a nice entry and 0 is a hard cut - but 0 is REQUIRED if you're going to move the camera every tick (an orbit, a chase, a dolly), because any other value restarts a whole new ease on every move and the shot rubber-bands. That rubber-band is the classic 'why is my camera jittery' bug.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the takeover happened. False means there was no camera to take over - almost always because player 1 was asked for in a single-player game.

nodes.title: Camera: Set Blend Time
nodes.desc: Arms how long the NEXT Place Camera takes to glide across, instead of cutting. Begin Cinematic sets this once at the start; use this to re-arm it for a later smooth move - swing the camera out to one side, then later swing it back. This is for one-off moves only, one Place Camera per blend. A camera you're moving every tick still wants 0 here or it rubber-bands.
nodes.desc_short: Arms how long the NEXT Place Camera takes to glide across, instead of cutting.

params.name: i
params.desc: Whose camera. 0 is you.

params.name: nDur
params.desc: Seconds the next camera move takes. 1 is a gentle glide, 2 to 3 is stately, 0 is an instant cut.

nodes.title: Camera: End Cinematic (Gives Control Back)
nodes.desc: Hands the camera and the player's controls back, and stops any watch or orbit follow loop running for that player. This is the way out of EVERY camera takeover - make certain something reaches it, on every path through your script. If a shot is already running and you have no way to get here, use Panic Revert.
nodes.desc_short: Hands the camera and the player's controls back, and stops any watch or orbit follow loop running for that...

params.name: i
params.desc: Whose camera to release. 0 is you. Releasing a player who was never taken over is harmless.

nodes.title: Camera: Fade Screen
nodes.desc: Fades the whole screen to black, or back to clear - the standard bookend for a cutscene, and the trick for hiding a cut or a teleport. There is no duration on this call at any confirmed use, so it is a straight set: use two of them with a wait between for a fade out then in. Careful - a fade to black with nothing to clear it leaves the player staring at nothing, so always have a clearing step (the cutscene runtime clears it for you automatically when a scene ends).
nodes.desc_short: Fades the whole screen to black, or back to clear - the standard bookend for a cutscene, and the trick for...

params.name: nAmount
params.desc: How black the screen is: 0 is fully clear, 1 is fully black. Those are the only two values real game code is confirmed to use.

nodes.title: Camera: Follow A Hardpoint
nodes.desc: Keeps the camera glued to a named hardpoint on a MOVING object by re-reading that point's world position many times a second and pushing the camera there - the fallback for the cases where the engine's own object-and-bone camera form does nothing. IMPORTANT: a look-at binding must already be active (run Look At A Point (Anchor), or a cinematic look-at, first) or setting the camera's position silently does nothing, exactly as everywhere else in this namespace. This is not a fix for the vehicle GUNNER camera - while seated in a turret the camera you can reach isn't the active one at all, which is a known hard limit.
nodes.desc_short: Keeps the camera glued to a named hardpoint on a MOVING object by re-reading that point's world position many...

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The object carrying the hardpoint to follow.

params.name: hp
params.desc: The name of the bone or hardpoint to sit the camera on. Bone_Head works on a person; vehicles use their own hp_ names.

params.name: i
params.desc: Which player's camera to move. 0 is you.

params.name: interval
params.desc: How often to re-read the point, in seconds. 0.05 (twenty times a second) is the default and looks smooth; bigger numbers are cheaper but choppier.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: KEEP this. Call it (or drop it into an Ess Stop node) to end the follow - otherwise it keeps dragging the camera around forever.

nodes.title: Camera: Set Field Of View
nodes.desc: Blends the camera's field of view to a new angle over a few seconds - a punchy zoom in, or a wide dramatic pull back. Heads up: this reaches a genuinely DIFFERENT engine system from every other camera node here (it takes a player slot number rather than a camera handle) - it lives with the camera nodes because it is a camera effect, not because it shares any plumbing. Always pair it with Restore Field Of View or the player is left zoomed forever.
nodes.desc_short: Blends the camera's field of view to a new angle over a few seconds - a punchy zoom in, or a wide dramatic...

params.name: i
params.desc: Which player slot. Every confirmed real use in the game's own scripts passes 0, the local player.

params.name: nAngle
params.desc: The new field of view angle. Smaller zooms IN (30 is a strong telephoto look), larger pulls back to a wide, warped view. The game's normal value isn't documented anywhere confirmed, so set a value, look at it, adjust.

params.name: nDuration
params.desc: Seconds to blend to the new angle. 1 is a smooth push; 0 snaps instantly.

nodes.title: Camera: Hold Framing
nodes.desc: Pins the shot exactly where it is now, so the camera stops easing and stays on the framing you set. Use it as the last step of a locked-off shot: place the camera, aim it, hold it. End Cinematic releases the hold along with everything else.
nodes.desc_short: Pins the shot exactly where it is now, so the camera stops easing and stays on the framing you set.

params.name: i
params.desc: Whose camera to pin. 0 is you.

nodes.title: Camera: Look At A Point (Anchor)
nodes.desc: The fix for the single biggest camera trap on this engine: moving the camera does NOTHING until the camera has been told to look at an OBJECT - not even a deliberately huge test teleport moves it without one. This spawns a tiny invisible marker at a spot and locks the camera onto it, which creates that binding for real. After that you re-aim the shot by moving the marker, and clean up by removing it. It uses a TinyGeometry marker on purpose: that one is confirmed safe during live gameplay, unlike the 'Verification Camera' prop, which the game calls in and despawns almost immediately unless the world is paused.
nodes.desc_short: The fix for the single biggest camera trap on this engine: moving the camera does NOTHING until the camera...

params.name: x
params.desc: East/west coordinate of the spot to look at. Usually wired in from a position node rather than typed.

params.name: y
params.desc: Height of the spot. Aim about head height on a person rather than at their feet.

params.name: z
params.desc: North/south coordinate of the spot to look at.

params.name: i
params.desc: Which player's camera to bind. 0 is you; 1 is the co-op partner and does nothing in single-player.

returns.name: uAnchor
returns.desc: The little marker that was created. KEEP it: move it to re-aim the shot, and remove it when you're done or it stays in the world forever. You get nothing back if that player has no camera.

nodes.title: Camera: Look At An Object
nodes.desc: Locks the camera onto a thing and KEEPS it framed as that thing moves - this is the 'watch the helicopter fly in' shot, and the engine does the panning itself, so it stays smooth for free. It also creates the look-at binding that Place Camera needs before it will do anything. Tracking a moving VEHICLE: aim at whoever is RIDING it and give the bone Bone_Chest, because object tracking works on character bones, not vehicle hardpoints. Needs a camera takeover (Begin Cinematic) to be in effect.
nodes.desc_short: Locks the camera onto a thing and KEEPS it framed as that thing moves - this is the 'watch the helicopter fly...

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The thing to keep framed. Wire in whatever you spawned - a helicopter, a car, a person.

params.name: sBone
params.desc: Optional bone or hardpoint to frame instead of the object's centre - Bone_Chest keeps a rider or a talking character nicely framed. Leave empty to look at the object as a whole.

params.name: i
params.desc: Whose camera. 0 is you.

nodes.title: Camera: Look At A Fixed Point
nodes.desc: Aims the camera at a fixed spot in the world by coordinates. WARNING, confirmed trap: this coordinate form does NOT create the look-at binding the engine needs, so Place Camera afterwards can silently do nothing and leave the camera stuck on the player - with control frozen, watching yourself. If you are placing the camera yourself, use Look At A Point (Anchor) instead, which spawns a tiny marker and looks at that; the cutscene runtime routes all of its point shots that way for exactly this reason.
nodes.desc_short: Aims the camera at a fixed spot in the world by coordinates.

params.name: x
params.desc: East/west coordinate of the spot to aim at.

params.name: y
params.desc: Height of the spot to aim at.

params.name: z
params.desc: North/south coordinate of the spot to aim at.

params.name: i
params.desc: Whose camera. 0 is you.

nodes.title: Camera: Panic Revert (Escape Hatch)
nodes.desc: The always-works way out. Force-releases EVERY camera takeover, for every player, and hands control back. Even while a cutscene has the controls locked the Lua console still accepts commands, so this can be fired blind to rescue a stuck camera. Worth putting on a key while you're building shots - it is the difference between a bad shot and a quit-to-desktop.
nodes.desc_short: The always-works way out.

nodes.title: Camera: Place Camera
nodes.desc: Puts the cinematic camera at a fixed spot in the world. Two things must already be true or it silently does nothing at all: the camera must be taken over (Begin Cinematic), and it must already be looking at an OBJECT - so run Look At An Object or Look At A Point (Anchor) FIRST, then place. Whether the camera cuts or glides there is set by the blend time, not by this node.
nodes.desc_short: Puts the cinematic camera at a fixed spot in the world.

params.name: x
params.desc: East/west coordinate of the vantage point. Normally wired in from a position node, offset a bit so you're not standing inside your subject.

params.name: y
params.desc: Height of the vantage point. Adding 8 to 12 above ground level gives the classic looking-down establishing shot.

params.name: z
params.desc: North/south coordinate of the vantage point.

params.name: i
params.desc: Whose camera to move. 0 is you.

nodes.title: Camera: Restore Field Of View
nodes.desc: Blends the field of view back to the game's normal value after Set Field Of View. Nothing else undoes it, so every zoom needs one of these eventually.
nodes.desc_short: Blends the field of view back to the game's normal value after Set Field Of View.

params.name: i
params.desc: Which player slot - the same one you zoomed. 0 is the local player.

params.name: nDuration
params.desc: Seconds to blend back. 1 is smooth; 0 snaps.

nodes.title: Camera: Shake
nodes.desc: Rattles the screen - the instant way to sell an explosion, a crash or a heavy impact. The default preset is a one-shot medium shake that ends by itself, which is the safe choice for a single call. The other confirmed preset keeps going until something stops it.
nodes.desc_short: Rattles the screen - the instant way to sell an explosion, a crash or a heavy impact.

params.name: i
params.desc: Whose camera shakes. 0 is you; 1 is the co-op partner and does nothing in single-player.

params.name: sPreset
params.desc: The named shake style. ShakeCameraMedium is a one-shot rattle that stops on its own. ShakeCameraConstantlyRandom runs until the Stop Shake node is used - left unstopped it shakes until the player leaves the level. Those two are the names confirmed to exist.

params.name: uSource
params.desc: What the shake is coming from, so the game can judge it against the camera. Point it at the explosion, or just at the player.

params.name: nAmplitude
params.desc: How hard the shake is. 6 is the default and reads clearly - push it up for a big blast, down for a background rumble.

params.name: nDuration
params.desc: How many seconds it lasts. Meaningless for the never-ending preset, which needs Stop Shake instead.

nodes.title: Camera: Stop Shake
nodes.desc: Switches off an ongoing ShakeCameraConstantlyRandom shake. The one-shot medium shake finishes by itself and never needs this - but a constant shake left running lasts until the player leaves the level, so always pair the two.
nodes.desc_short: Switches off an ongoing ShakeCameraConstantlyRandom shake.

params.name: i
params.desc: Whose camera to settle. 0 is you.

params.name: uSource
params.desc: The same source you gave the Shake node.

nodes.title: Cinematic: Define A Named Cutscene
nodes.desc: Registers a cutscene under a name so it can be played later from anywhere by that name - a mission intro, a trigger, a contract. Nothing plays until you use Play A Named Cutscene. Definitions are wiped every time the game loads a level, on purpose, so that a saved scene can never carry stale coordinates into a different map - re-register yours when your script loads.
nodes.desc_short: Registers a cutscene under a name so it can be played later from anywhere by that name - a mission intro, a...

params.name: id
params.desc: The name you'll play it by. Keep it short and recognisable - defining a second scene with the same name replaces the first.

params.name: steps
params.default: { { type = "orbit", target = "player", radius = 9, height = 4, speed = 45, hold = 6 }, { type = "banner", text = "Reinforcements inbound", hold = 2 } }
params.desc: The storyboard, same shape as the Play node: a Lua list of steps, each with type =, its own settings, and hold = seconds to wait before the next one.

params.name: opts
params.desc: Default settings for this scene (camera, blend, skippable, skipKey, startFade, i, onDone). Play A Named Cutscene can override any of them for one particular play.

nodes.title: Cinematic: Is A Cutscene Playing
nodes.desc: Tells you whether a cutscene is running right now. Only one can play at a time and a new one cancels the old, so this is the guard to put in front of anything that starts a scene - a second press of the key then does nothing instead of cutting the first scene short.
nodes.desc_short: Tells you whether a cutscene is running right now.

returns.name: bPlaying
returns.desc: True while a cutscene is running, false otherwise.

nodes.title: Cinematic: Play A Cutscene
nodes.desc: Plays an ordered list of steps as a cutscene - camera cuts, dollies, orbits and chases, spawns, AI orders, narration, fades, shakes, music, teleports - each step waiting its own 'hold' seconds before the next. By default it TAKES OVER the screen and the player's controls, and it ALWAYS gives them back when the scene finishes, is skipped, or is stopped; a step that errors is logged and the timeline carries on, and the screen is always cleared of any fade at the end, so a cutscene can never strand the player. Pressing ESC skips: every remaining step still FIRES (so actors the scene was going to spawn or position all still end up in place), it just stops waiting between them. Starting a new cutscene cancels any one already running.
nodes.desc_short: Plays an ordered list of steps as a cutscene - camera cuts, dollies, orbits and chases, spawns, AI orders,...

params.name: steps
params.default: { { type = "orbit", target = "player", radius = 9, height = 4, speed = 45, hold = 6 }, { type = "banner", text = "Reinforcements inbound", hold = 2 } }
params.desc: The storyboard: a Lua list of steps in order. Each is a table with type =, its own settings, and hold = how many seconds to wait before the next one (hold 0 fires the next step on the same tick, so several things can start together). Types: camera, orbit, chase, wait, spawn, face, order, fly, say/banner, subtitle, hint, vo, music, sound, fade, shake, teleport, relations, func. A spawn step's name = registers that actor so later steps can refer to it by that label, and "player" always means the hero.

params.name: opts
params.desc: Scene settings: camera = false runs the timeline WITHOUT taking over the screen, blend (0 for instant cuts, the default), skippable (ESC fast-forwards - on unless you turn it off), skipKey, startFade = true to open on black, i for the player index, and onDone = a function that runs when the scene ends.

returns.name: seq
returns.desc: A handle for the running scene. You can leave this unwired - the Stop node with nothing wired already ends whichever scene is playing. You get nothing back if the steps weren't a proper list.

nodes.title: Cinematic: Play A Named Cutscene
nodes.desc: Plays a cutscene you registered with Define A Named Cutscene. Same behaviour as playing one directly: it takes over the screen, ESC skips it, and control always comes back at the end. If no scene by that name exists, nothing happens and a line is written to the log - check your spelling and that the define ran first, since definitions are cleared on every level load.
nodes.desc_short: Plays a cutscene you registered with Define A Named Cutscene.

params.name: id
params.desc: The name the scene was defined under.

params.name: extraOpts
params.desc: Settings that override the defined ones for this play only - most often onDone, so the same scene can run different code each time it ends. Leave empty to use the scene's own settings.

returns.name: seq
returns.desc: A handle for the running scene. Safe to leave unwired - Stop with nothing wired ends whatever is playing. You get nothing back if no scene by that name was defined.

nodes.title: Cinematic: Skip To The End
nodes.desc: Fast-forwards the cutscene that's playing: every remaining step still fires straight away, so everything the scene was going to spawn, order or say still happens - it simply stops waiting between them. This is exactly what ESC does for the player; use this node to skip from your own code, such as a button or a trigger. To end a scene WITHOUT firing the rest of it, use Stop instead.
nodes.desc_short: Fast-forwards the cutscene that's playing: every remaining step still fires straight away, so everything the...

nodes.title: Cinematic: Stop A Cutscene
nodes.desc: Ends the cutscene immediately. Remaining steps do NOT fire. The camera and controls go back to the player, any fade is cleared so the screen can't be left black, any tutorial hint is hidden, anything the scene marked as temporary is cleaned up, and the scene's onDone code runs. Use Skip instead when you want the rest of the scene's actions to still take effect.
nodes.desc_short: Ends the cutscene immediately.

params.name: seq
params.desc: Leave this empty. With nothing here it stops whichever cutscene is currently playing, which is what you almost always want; it only exists so code holding one specific scene handle can end that one.

nodes.title: Color: From Hex Code
nodes.desc: Turns a web colour code like #ff8800 into the red, green and blue numbers (0-255) that Ess markers and UI panels expect. Accepts #RRGGBB, RRGGBB, or the three-letter short form #f80. Gives back nothing at all if the text isn't a valid colour, so check it before using it.
nodes.desc_short: Turns a web colour code like #ff8800 into the red, green and blue numbers (0-255) that Ess markers and UI...

params.name: s
params.desc: The hex colour code, with or without the leading #.

returns.name: r
returns.desc: Red, 0-255 (nothing if the code was invalid).

returns.name: g
returns.desc: Green, 0-255.

nodes.promoted_from_getter: multi-value return cannot be spliced inline as an expression

nodes.title: Color: From Hue/Saturation/Value
nodes.desc: Builds a colour from hue, saturation and brightness instead of red/green/blue - the easy way to make a rainbow, or to give every squad member a clearly different tint by stepping the hue round. Hue is degrees around the colour wheel (0 red, 120 green, 240 blue); saturation and value run 0 to 1.
nodes.desc_short: Builds a colour from hue, saturation and brightness instead of red/green/blue - the easy way to make a...

params.name: h
params.desc: Hue in degrees, 0 to 360 around the colour wheel.

params.name: s
params.desc: Saturation, 0 (grey) to 1 (vivid).

params.name: v
params.desc: Brightness, 0 (black) to 1 (full).

returns.name: g
returns.desc: Green, 0-255.

nodes.promoted_from_getter: multi-value return cannot be spliced inline as an expression

nodes.title: Color: Blend
nodes.desc: Blends two colours together - the trick behind a health bar that slides from green through yellow to red. Each colour is typed as a { r, g, b } list; t of 0 gives the first colour, 1 gives the second, and anything outside 0..1 is pulled back in.
nodes.desc_short: Blends two colours together - the trick behind a health bar that slides from green through yellow to red.

params.name: c1
params.desc: First colour as { r, g, b }, each 0-255.

params.name: c2
params.desc: Second colour as { r, g, b }, each 0-255.

params.name: t
params.desc: How far between them, 0 to 1.

returns.name: r
returns.desc: Red of the blended colour, 0-255.

returns.name: g
returns.desc: Green of the blended colour, 0-255.

returns.name: b
returns.desc: Blue of the blended colour, 0-255.

nodes.promoted_from_getter: multi-value return cannot be spliced inline as an expression

nodes.title: Color: By Name
nodes.desc: Looks up a ready-made colour by name so you never have to remember numbers. Known names: red, green, blue, yellow, orange, cyan, magenta, purple, pink, lime, teal, white, black, gray (or grey) and brown. Capitals don't matter. An unrecognised name gives back nothing.
nodes.desc_short: Looks up a ready-made colour by name so you never have to remember numbers.

params.name: name
params.desc: A colour name, e.g. "orange".

returns.name: r
returns.desc: Red, 0-255 (nothing if the name is unknown).

returns.name: g
returns.desc: Green, 0-255.

nodes.promoted_from_getter: multi-value return cannot be spliced inline as an expression

nodes.title: Contract: Cancel Mission
nodes.desc: Stops the running mission immediately and counts it as failed - no reward, the fail callback fires. Everything the mission created is cleaned up: HUD objective lines cleared, mission-spawned units and markers removed, faction stances put back the way they were, special music stopped. Safe to call when nothing is running (it just does nothing). This is your panic button while testing a mission.
nodes.desc_short: Stops the running mission immediately and counts it as failed - no reward, the fail callback fires.

nodes.title: Contract: Start Mission
nodes.desc: Starts a registered mission and hands the player their first objective. Places the heroes if the definition has a `start`, sets faction stances, plays the intro cutscene if there is one, then runs the objectives (in order, or all at once in parallel mode) until they are all done or one fails. Only one contract runs at a time - accepting a new one aborts whatever was running. In co-op only the host runs missions; a joining client is skipped on purpose.
nodes.desc_short: Starts a registered mission and hands the player their first objective.

params.name: idOrDef
params.desc: The id you gave the mission when you registered it. (It also accepts a whole mission definition table directly, if you would rather skip registering.)

nodes.title: Contract: Chase Objective
nodes.desc: Build a runner: targets that are actively trying to escape. It finds its targets the same three ways Destroy does (spawn them, name placed ones, or sweep an area), marks them, then ORDERS each one to run or drive for the escape point at whatever urgency you set - for a vehicle it steers the driver, not the hull, so they actually go. Kill all of them to complete. If even one reaches the escape point, or the optional clock runs out, the mission fails. This is your fleeing convoy or escaping VIP.
nodes.desc_short: Build a runner: targets that are actively trying to escape.

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Stop the fleeing convoy', spawns = { { 'Veyron', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 }, { 'Veyron', -514, -2.1, 2706, 0 } }, escapeAt = { -440, -2.1, 2620 }, escapeRadius = 20, haste = 2, time = 120 }
params.desc: The objective spec. Targets come from `spawns` (a list of `{template, x, y, z, yaw}`), `objects = {'name', ...}` or `where = {area={x,y,z,r}, kind=, faction=}` - same as Destroy. `escapeAt = {x, y, z}` is where they are running to and `escapeRadius` is how close they need to get to have escaped (default 15). `haste` sets how hard they run (1 is normal, higher is faster). `time` is an optional deadline in seconds.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: Collect Objective
nodes.desc: Build a pickup run. It spawns each item you list as a physical object in the world and marks it, and the player collects one simply by walking up to it - get within the pickup radius and it vanishes and the count goes up. Completes once the quota is reached. Good for intel, crates, cash drops and fetch quests.
nodes.desc_short: Build a pickup run. It spawns each item you list as a physical object in the world and marks it, and the...

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Collect 3 intel packets', items = { { 'Veyron', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 }, { 'Veyron', -512, -2.1, 2706, 0 }, { 'Veyron', -504, -2.1, 2712, 0 } }, quota = 3, radius = 4 }
params.desc: The objective spec. `items` is a list of `{template, x, y, z, yaw}` pickups to spawn (use whatever prop template reads as your collectible). `quota` is how many the player needs (default: all of them). `radius` is how close they must get to grab one, in metres - defaults to 4, which is roughly 'walk over it'.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: Defend Objective
nodes.desc: Build a 'hold out and keep it alive' objective. A clock runs for the given number of seconds; when it runs out the objective is complete. If the thing you named as the target is destroyed before then, the whole mission FAILS. With no target it is simply a survive-the-clock objective. Pair it with reinforcement waves from the contract's `support` list to give the player something to actually defend against.
nodes.desc_short: Build a 'hold out and keep it alive' objective.

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Defend the transmitter for 60 seconds', time = 60, target = 'transmitter' }
params.desc: The objective spec. `desc` is the HUD line, `time` is how many seconds to hold (defaults to 60), and `target` is the NAME of an object already placed in the level - if it dies, the mission fails. Leave `target` out for a plain timer.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: Destroy Objective
nodes.desc: Build a 'wreck these targets' objective. It can SPAWN its own targets for you (`spawns`), point at objects already placed in the level by name (`objects`), or sweep everything of a kind inside an area (`where`) - or any mix. Every target gets marked on the radar, PDA and in the world, and the objective completes once enough of them are destroyed. Anything it spawned is removed automatically when the mission ends. If it resolves zero targets it just completes instantly rather than hanging the mission.
nodes.desc_short: Build a 'wreck these targets' objective.

params.name: t
params.desc: The objective spec. `desc` is the line the player reads on the HUD. `spawns` is a list of `{template, x, y, z, yaw}` targets to create (swap in your own coordinates - stand where you want them and read the numbers with Ess.Player.pose(0)). `objects = {'name', ...}` uses already-placed level objects instead. `where = {area={x,y,z,r}, kind='vehicles', faction='VZ'}` grabs whatever is there right now. `quota` = how many must die (default: all of them). Every objective builder also takes `msg` (a radio line when it starts) and, inside a parallel group, `optional = true` plus `bonus = 5000` for a cash side-goal.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: Get In Vehicle Objective
nodes.desc: Build a 'get in that vehicle' objective. It either points at a vehicle already placed in the level or spawns one for you, marks it so the player can find it, and completes the moment a player character sits down in the chosen seat. Worth knowing: this is the one objective type the framework has deliberately never live-tested (it needs a real player physically boarding a vehicle), so test it in-game before you build a mission around it.
nodes.desc_short: Build a 'get in that vehicle' objective.

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Get in the chopper', spawn = { 'Ka29b (Full)', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 }, seat = 'd' }
params.desc: The objective spec. Either `target = 'name'` for a vehicle already in the level, or `spawn = {template, x, y, z, yaw}` to create one. `seat` picks which seat counts - 'd' is the driver's seat and is the default.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: Escort Objective
nodes.desc: Build an escort objective. It spawns the thing to be escorted, marks it as a friendly to protect, and completes when THAT thing reaches the destination point. If it is destroyed on the way, the mission fails. One important catch: this objective only spawns and watches - it never gives the escortee movement orders, so in practice it should be a vehicle the player actually drives to the destination, or something ordered around by the contract's own units and waypoints.
nodes.desc_short: Build an escort objective.

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Get the truck to the safehouse', spawn = { 'Veyron', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 }, to = { -440, -2.1, 2620 }, radius = 15 }
params.desc: The objective spec. `spawn = {template, x, y, z, yaw}` creates the escortee. `to = {x, y, z}` is the destination and `radius` is how close it has to get (defaults to 15). The destination is marked with a ground ring for the player.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: Extraction Objective
nodes.desc: Build the exfil - the objective that ends a mission. It marks the landing zone and completes once the player gets out. With a board time of 0 the LZ itself is the finish line; give it a board time and the player must hold the LZ that many seconds while the pick-up comes in (stepping out resets the count), optionally with a chopper spawning on the pad. Add a victory lap and instead of just cutting to complete, the player is seated as a PASSENGER in that chopper and flown a couple of orbits over the wreckage with a free camera - no cutscene takeover, they can look around at what they did.
nodes.desc_short: Build the exfil - the objective that ends a mission.

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Fall back to the LZ and extract', at = { -522.10, -2.09, 2697.43 }, radius = 12, boardTime = 2, heli = 'Mi26 (CH) (Driver)', victoryLap = { orbits = 2, radius = 110, height = 55, line = "Rig's ours. Let's take her home." } }
params.desc: The objective spec. `at = {x, y, z}` and `radius` (default 15) are the LZ. `boardTime` is seconds to hold it (0 = instant extract, no chopper needed). `heli` names a chopper template to spawn on the pad - for a victory lap it must be a CREWED template (one with a driver, like 'Mi26 (CH) (Driver)'), or nobody flies it. `victoryLap = {orbits, radius, height, line}` flies the exit lap; `line` is a radio send-off.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: Objective Group (Phase)
nodes.desc: Bundle several objectives into ONE - a mission phase. To the mission this counts as a single objective, but inside it you can run its children one after another ('sequential', the default) or all at the same time ('parallel'). A parallel group finishes when every non-optional child is done, and fails the moment a required child fails. This is how you say 'do these three things in any order, then move on', or how you build a mission in acts. Groups can be nested inside groups.
nodes.desc_short: Bundle several objectives into ONE - a mission phase.

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Secure the compound', mode = 'parallel', objectives = { Ess.Contract.Destroy{ desc = 'Wreck the AA gun', spawns = { { 'Veyron', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 } } }, Ess.Contract.Reach{ desc = 'Tag the fuel depot', at = { -500, -2.1, 2680 }, radius = 10 }, Ess.Contract.Hold{ desc = 'Bonus: hold the roof', at = { -510, -2.1, 2690 }, radius = 12, time = 20, optional = true, bonus = 2500 } } }
params.desc: The objective spec. `objectives` is the list of child objective nodes. `mode` is 'sequential' (default, one after another) or 'parallel' (all at once). In parallel mode a child marked `optional = true` never blocks the group, and if it also has `bonus = 2500` the player is paid that cash for finishing it.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: Hold Position Objective
nodes.desc: Build a 'hold this ground' objective. The zone is marked with a ground ring, and a timer counts up only while the player is standing inside it. Reach the required number of seconds and it completes. Time inside ADDS UP - stepping out of the ring pauses the count rather than wiping it, so a player who ducks out for cover does not lose all their progress. Pair it with reinforcement waves from the contract's `support` list for a classic capture-the-point fight.
nodes.desc_short: Build a 'hold this ground' objective.

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Hold the landing zone for 30 seconds', at = { -524.02, -2.1, 2714.44 }, radius = 20, time = 30 }
params.desc: The objective spec. `at = {x, y, z}` and `radius` (defaults to 15) define the ring the player must stand in; `time` is how many seconds of standing there it takes (defaults to 15).

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: Interact Objective
nodes.desc: Build a 'go and use this' objective - plant a charge, hack a terminal, talk to a contact, sabotage a generator, cut a prisoner loose. The action itself is imaginary: the flavour lives entirely in the wording you give it. The player has to get close to the target (or the bare spot) and STAY there while a short hold timer runs; walking away resets the hold to zero, so they have to commit. A hold time of 0 completes the moment they arrive.
nodes.desc_short: Build a 'go and use this' objective - plant a charge, hack a terminal, talk to a contact, sabotage a...

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Plant the charge on the refinery core', at = { -526.89, -2.10, 2737.72 }, radius = 6, time = 2 }
params.desc: The objective spec. Point it at a place with `at = {x, y, z}` (a ground ring is drawn there), at an object already in the level with `target = 'name'`, or at something to create with `spawn = {template, x, y, z, yaw}`. `radius` is how close counts (defaults to 4) and `time` is how many seconds they must stand there (defaults to 0 = instant).

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: List Registered Missions
nodes.desc: Gives you every mission definition registered so far, in the order they were registered - the raw material for a mission-select board or a debug menu. The list is rebuilt from scratch on every level load, because nothing about a contract is ever written into the save.
nodes.desc_short: Gives you every mission definition registered so far, in the order they were registered - the raw material...

returns.name: missions
returns.desc: An array of the registered definition tables (each with its `id`, `title`, `briefing`, `reward`, and so on).

nodes.title: Contract: Protect (Fail Condition)
nodes.desc: A background FAIL CONDITION, not a goal - it belongs in the contract's `fail` list, never in `objectives`. It watches one unit for the entire mission, marks it as a friendly, and instantly fails the whole mission the moment it dies. It can never complete on its own; it just sits there in the background the whole time. Use it for 'the convoy must survive' or 'do not let the hostage die' rules that apply across every objective.
nodes.desc_short: A background FAIL CONDITION, not a goal - it belongs in the contract's `fail` list, never in `objectives`.

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Keep the hostage alive', spawn = { 'Allied Officer', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 } }
params.desc: The spec. Either `target = 'name'` for something already placed in the level, or `spawn = {template, x, y, z, yaw}` to create it. `desc` is just documentation here - a fail condition never draws its own HUD line.

returns.name: condition
returns.desc: Put this in the contract's `fail` list (not `objectives`).

nodes.title: Contract: Race Objective
nodes.desc: Build a checkpoint run. Only the NEXT checkpoint is marked at any time, so the player is always chasing one ring; hit it and the marker jumps to the following one. It completes when they have gone through all of them in order, and the finishing time is logged. Set a par time and blowing it fails the mission - that is your street-race or timed-delivery objective.
nodes.desc_short: Build a checkpoint run.

params.name: t
params.desc: The objective spec. `checkpoints` is a list of `{x, y, z}` points in the order they must be crossed. `radius` is how wide each gate is, in metres (defaults to 12 - keep it generous for vehicles). `time` is an optional par time in seconds; run out and the mission fails.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: Reach Objective
nodes.desc: Build a 'get to this place' objective - the simplest one there is. It draws a ground ring and a destination blip at the point so the player can see where to go, and completes the instant a player walks or drives inside the radius. Nothing to kill, nothing to spawn.
nodes.desc_short: Build a 'get to this place' objective - the simplest one there is.

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Reach the extraction point', at = { -522.1, -2.09, 2697.43 }, radius = 12 }
params.desc: The objective spec. `desc` is the HUD line, `at = {x, y, z}` is the spot (replace these coordinates with your own - stand there and read them with Ess.Player.pose(0)), and `radius` is how close counts, in metres (defaults to 15). Anything under about 8 gets fiddly in a vehicle.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: Register Mission
nodes.desc: Files a whole mission definition under an id so it can be started later. This is the heavyweight of the three mission tools: a full engine with 16 objective types, rewards, spawned units, triggers and support call-ins. A contract is EPHEMERAL - it is built only from safe primitives and never writes anything into your game save, so it can never corrupt one; the trade-off is that it does not survive a save/reload, it is simply re-offered next time the level loads. Registering does not start anything: follow it with Accept.
nodes.desc_short: Files a whole mission definition under an id so it can be started later.

params.name: def
params.default: { id = 'my_first_mission', title = 'Clear the Yard', briefing = 'Wreck the two cars, then reach the extraction point.', reward = { cash = 5000, fuel = 50 }, objectives = { Ess.Contract.Destroy{ desc = 'Destroy the 2 cars', spawns = { { 'Veyron', -520, -2.1, 2700, 0 }, { 'Veyron', -510, -2.1, 2700, 0 } } }, Ess.Contract.Reach{ desc = 'Reach the extraction point', at = { -522.1, -2.09, 2697.43 }, radius = 12 } }, onComplete = function() Ess.Log('mission complete, reward paid') end }
params.desc: The mission definition. Only `id` is truly required (and it should have `objectives` or nothing will happen). Common keys: `title`/`briefing` (text), `reward = {cash=, fuel=}`, `objectives = { ...objective nodes... }`, `mode = 'parallel'` to run them all at once instead of in order, `start = {x,y,z,yaw}` to place the heroes when it begins, `timeLimit` in seconds, `fail = { Protect/StayInArea nodes }`, `intro` (an opening radio line), `onComplete`/`onFail` functions. Bigger missions add `units`, `waypoints`, `support`, `triggers`, `relations`, `cinematic` and `sandbox = true`.

nodes.title: Contract: Mission Status
nodes.desc: Reads how the current mission is going - which objectives are ticked off, overall progress, and how much time is left on a time limit. Returns nothing at all when no mission is running. After a mission ends the last result stays readable (until the next Accept) so you can check whether it was completed or failed.
nodes.desc_short: Reads how the current mission is going - which objectives are ticked off, overall progress, and how much time...

returns.name: status
returns.desc: A table: `objectives` (a list of `{done = true/false}`, one per objective), `progress` (0 to 1), `timeLeft` (seconds, only with a time limit), and `finished` ('complete' or 'failed') once it is over. Nil if no mission has run.

nodes.title: Contract: Stay In Area (Fail Condition)
nodes.desc: A background FAIL CONDITION, not a goal - it belongs in the contract's `fail` list, never in `objectives`. It fails the mission the instant the player leaves a circle around the given point: the classic 'do not leave the mission area' leash, running quietly under every objective. Note it draws NO marker or boundary of any kind, so say where the edge is in the mission briefing or the player will just get failed with no warning.
nodes.desc_short: A background FAIL CONDITION, not a goal - it belongs in the contract's `fail` list, never in `objectives`.

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Do not leave the refinery grounds', at = { -522.10, -2.09, 2697.43 }, radius = 250 }
params.desc: The spec. `at = {x, y, z}` is the centre of the allowed area and `radius` is how far the player may stray, in metres. The default radius if you omit it is only 100, which is very tight for anything with a vehicle in it - a few hundred is usually fairer.

returns.name: condition
returns.desc: Put this in the contract's `fail` list (not `objectives`).

nodes.title: Contract: Survive Objective
nodes.desc: Build a 'stay alive until the clock runs out' objective. This one draws its OWN countdown on the HUD ('Hold out (23s)') so the player watches the seconds tick down, and completes when it hits zero. You can also name something that must survive alongside them - if it dies first the mission fails. Almost always paired with enemy waves fired from the contract's `support` list, otherwise the player just stands around for a minute.
nodes.desc_short: Build a 'stay alive until the clock runs out' objective.

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Hold out until evac arrives', time = 45 }
params.desc: The objective spec. `time` is the countdown in seconds (defaults to 60). `target` is optional and names something that must not die - either a group name from the contract's own `units` list, or the name of an object placed in the level.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Contract: HVT Bounty Objective
nodes.desc: Build a bounty on one named individual - a high-value target. It marks them and completes when they are killed. Turn on capture and there is a second way to finish it: get right up next to them while they are badly wounded and they count as taken alive instead, which is how you build a 'bring them in' contract without needing a real subdue animation.
nodes.desc_short: Build a bounty on one named individual - a high-value target.

params.name: t
params.default: { desc = 'Take out the Allied boss', spawn = { 'Allied Boss', -535.11, -2.15, 2706.61, 21.84 }, capture = true, captureHealth = 25, radius = 3 }
params.desc: The objective spec. Either `target = 'name'` for someone already placed in the level, or `spawn = {template, x, y, z, yaw}` to create them. `capture = true` also allows taking them alive: standing within `radius` metres (default 3) while their health is at or below `captureHealth` (default 25) counts as verified.

returns.name: objective
returns.desc: Pass this into a contract's objectives list.

nodes.title: Easy AI Orders: Attack
nodes.desc: Point a group of units at something and turn them loose - they hunt it down and open fire. Works on any units you hold guids for; they don't have to be your followers.
nodes.desc_short: Point a group of units at something and turn them loose - they hunt it down and open fire.

params.name: guids
params.desc: The units to command, as a Lua list of guids - normally the list a spawn node handed you. The default spawns three soldiers ahead of you (without setting them on you yet) so this node does something on its own.

params.name: target
params.desc: Who they go after. Ess.Player.character(0) is you, for a guaranteed instant firefight. Wire in any character or vehicle guid instead.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out.

nodes.title: Easy AI Orders: Guard
nodes.desc: They plant themselves on a spot and fight anything that comes inside it. This is the friendlier name for the engine's defend behaviour. Guarding has no natural finish - they hold that ground until you give them a different order.
nodes.desc_short: They plant themselves on a spot and fight anything that comes inside it.

params.name: guids
params.desc: The units to command, as a Lua list of guids - normally the list a spawn node handed you.

params.name: at
params.desc: The spot to hold, as {x, y, z}. The default { Ess.Player.pose(0) } means right where you're standing - Ess.Player.pose gives back your x, y, z (plus a yaw that's ignored here).

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out.

nodes.title: Easy AI Orders: Patrol
nodes.desc: They walk a beat between the points you list, over and over - a moving picket instead of a static guard. The route loops forever unless you drop down to Ess.AIOrders.command and pass loop = false.
nodes.desc_short: They walk a beat between the points you list, over and over - a moving picket instead of a static guard.

params.name: guids
params.desc: The units to command, as a Lua list of guids - normally the list a spawn node handed you.

params.name: points
params.desc: The route, as a list of {x, y, z} waypoints. Switch on Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read your own coordinates off the screen and paste real ones in here.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out.

nodes.title: Easy Airstrike: On a Spot
nodes.desc: A gunship screams over the spot and four artillery shells rain down on it a fraction of a second apart. This is real, lethal ordnance - don't call it on ground you're standing on.
nodes.desc_short: A gunship screams over the spot and four artillery shells rain down on it a fraction of a second apart.

params.name: x
params.desc: World X of the target spot. Use Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read coordinates off the screen.

params.name: y
params.desc: World Y (height/ground level) of the target spot.

params.name: z
params.desc: World Z of the target spot.

nodes.title: Easy Airstrike: On Me
nodes.desc: Calls the jet pass and the shell barrage down on your own head. For the brave, or for a cinematic - these are real explosives and they will kill you.
nodes.desc_short: Calls the jet pass and the shell barrage down on your own head.

params.name: i
params.desc: Player slot: 0 is you (the local player), 1 is your co-op partner.

nodes.title: Easy Airstrike: On My Target
nodes.desc: Whatever your crosshair is resting on takes the full treatment - a jet pass plus four shells on its position. Aim first, then fire this node. If your reticle isn't on anything, nothing happens at all.
nodes.desc_short: Whatever your crosshair is resting on takes the full treatment - a jet pass plus four shells on its position.

params.name: i
params.desc: Player slot whose reticle to read: 0 is you (the local player), 1 is your co-op partner.

nodes.title: Easy Camera: Fade In
nodes.desc: Fades the screen back up from black. The other half of Fade Out - always pair them, or you leave the player staring at a black screen.
nodes.desc_short: Fades the screen back up from black.

nodes.title: Easy Camera: Fade Out
nodes.desc: Slams the screen to black. Nothing else stops - the world keeps running behind it, and the player keeps their controls. Call Easy Camera: Fade In to bring the picture back.
nodes.desc_short: Slams the screen to black.

nodes.title: Easy Camera: Orbit a Target
nodes.desc: Takes over the camera and glides it in a slow circle around whatever you point it at - the money shot for showing off something you just spawned. WARNING: this steals the camera from the player until you call the stop function it hands back (or Ess.Camera.endCinematic), so always wire up a way out.
nodes.desc_short: Takes over the camera and glides it in a slow circle around whatever you point it at - the money shot for...

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The thing to circle. Ess.Player.character(0) orbits you; wire in a vehicle or character guid from a spawn node instead.

params.name: opts
params.desc: Optional dials: radius (how far out, default 12), height (above the target, 4), speed (degrees per second, 40), startAngle (0), look (a different guid to point the lens at), bone, i. The motion is damped by default so a fast target doesn't make the shot jitter - add smooth = false for the old exact snap, or smoothFactor from 0 to 1 (higher = snappier, lower = glassier).

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Call this to end the shot and hand the camera back to the player.

nodes.title: Easy Camera: Shake
nodes.desc: Kicks the screen around for a moment - the impact punch you want right after an explosion. Zero configuration: a medium shake centred on your character.
nodes.desc_short: Kicks the screen around for a moment - the impact punch you want right after an explosion.

params.name: i
params.desc: Player slot to shake: 0 is you (the local player), 1 is your co-op partner.

nodes.title: Easy Camera: Watch a Target
nodes.desc: Locks a cinematic camera onto something and keeps it framed as it moves - perfect for watching the helicopter you just spawned fly in. By default the camera sits still at a fixed vantage and pans to follow; set chase = true and it flies along behind instead. WARNING: this steals the camera from the player until you call the stop function it hands back.
nodes.desc_short: Locks a cinematic camera onto something and keeps it framed as it moves - perfect for watching the helicopter...

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The thing to keep in frame. Wire in the guid a spawn node handed you.

params.name: opts
params.desc: Optional dials: at = {x,y,z} (where the camera parks; default just above you), height (6), chase = true (fly along behind instead of panning), angle (chase viewpoint in degrees, 200), dist (chase distance, 16), chaseHeight (6), look (a different guid to frame), bone, i. GOTCHA: aiming at a moving VEHICLE doesn't track - point at whoever is riding it instead, e.g. { look = Ess.Vehicle.driver(heli), bone = "Bone_Chest" }.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Call this to end the shot and hand the camera back to the player.

nodes.title: Easy Cinematic: Play a Cutscene
nodes.desc: Plays a cutscene. Your steps fire in order, each held for its own few seconds, with the camera taken over and ESC letting the player skip. Control is ALWAYS handed back - on the last step, on a skip, or on a stop - so a cutscene can never strand the player. A skip still fires every remaining step (so actors a scene spawns end up in place), just with no waiting.
nodes.desc_short: Plays a cutscene. Your steps fire in order, each held for its own few seconds, with the camera taken over and...

params.name: steps
params.desc: The storyboard: a Lua list of step tables in play order. Ess.Easy.Cinematic.shot(...) builds the simplest one (a static camera shot). Steps can also be waits, spawns, AI orders, on-screen narration, fades, shakes, music and teleports - see Ess.Cinematic for the full set.

params.name: onDone
params.desc: Runs the moment the cutscene ends, whether it played out or the player skipped it. This is where you start the mission the scene was introducing.

returns.name: seq
returns.desc: The running sequence - hand it to Ess.Cinematic.stop to cut it short.

nodes.title: Easy Cinematic: Build One Shot
nodes.desc: Builds ONE static camera shot - lens parked at one point, aimed at another, held for a few seconds - ready to drop into a Play a Cutscene list. It doesn't play anything by itself; it just describes the shot, so a hand-written scene reads like a storyboard.
nodes.desc_short: Builds ONE static camera shot - lens parked at one point, aimed at another, held for a few seconds - ready to...

params.name: at
params.desc: Where the camera sits, as {x, y, z}.

params.name: lookAt
params.desc: The world point it aims at, as {x, y, z}.

params.name: seconds
params.desc: How long this shot is held before the scene cuts on. Default 3.

returns.name: step
returns.desc: One step table. Collect several into a list and hand them to Easy Cinematic: Play a Cutscene.

nodes.title: Easy UI: Yes/No Dialog
nodes.desc: Pops a yes/no dialog in front of the player and runs one of your two callbacks depending on which they pick.
nodes.desc_short: Pops a yes/no dialog in front of the player and runs one of your two callbacks depending on which they pick.

params.name: text
params.desc: The question shown in the dialog.

params.name: onYes
params.desc: What happens when they choose yes.

params.name: onNo
params.desc: What happens when they choose no. Optional - leave it out and a no simply does nothing.

nodes.title: Easy Console: Close
nodes.desc: Shuts the in-game Ess reference board, the playground and the search prompt - whichever of them is open.
nodes.desc_short: Shuts the in-game Ess reference board, the playground and the search prompt - whichever of them is open.

nodes.title: Easy Console: Open Reference
nodes.desc: Opens the in-game reference board: every Ess.Easy call in the framework, grouped by namespace, browsable with the D-pad and with a description for each. The node to reach for when you want to see what else is available without leaving the game.
nodes.desc_short: Opens the in-game reference board: every Ess.Easy call in the framework, grouped by namespace, browsable with...

nodes.title: Easy Console: Open Playground
nodes.desc: Opens the PLAYGROUND - a drill-down menu where you actually RUN framework calls live and cycle through their parameter values to watch what each one does. The fastest way to learn what a call looks like in game. Calling it a second time closes it again.
nodes.desc_short: Opens the PLAYGROUND - a drill-down menu where you actually RUN framework calls live and cycle through their...

nodes.title: Easy Console: Search Reference
nodes.desc: Opens a text prompt and filters the whole reference down to whatever you type, matching names, usage lines and descriptions (case doesn't matter). Submitting an empty search brings everything back.
nodes.desc_short: Opens a text prompt and filters the whole reference down to whatever you type, matching names, usage lines...

nodes.title: Easy Contract: Destroy Mission
nodes.desc: Registers a full kill-these-guys contract AND accepts it, in one node. The enemies spawn where you placed them, the mission shows up in the player's contract UI with its reward, and it completes when the last one is dead. Without this you'd have to learn Register, def.id and Accept just to get one mission running.
nodes.desc_short: Registers a full kill-these-guys contract AND accepts it, in one node.

params.name: sTitle
params.desc: The mission name the player sees in the contract UI.

params.name: tSpawns
params.desc: Who to spawn and where, as a list of {template, x, y, z} entries (an optional fifth number sets their facing). Killing all of them completes the contract.

params.name: tOpts
params.desc: Extras: desc (the objective line the player reads; defaults to the title) and reward = { cash = , fuel = }.

returns.name: id
returns.desc: The auto-generated contract id (easy1, easy2, ...) - keep it if you want to look this contract up later.

nodes.title: Easy Contract: Go-Here Mission
nodes.desc: Registers and accepts a go-here contract in one node: a real mission, in the player's contract UI, with a marked destination that completes the moment they arrive.
nodes.desc_short: Registers and accepts a go-here contract in one node: a real mission, in the player's contract UI, with a...

params.name: sTitle
params.desc: The mission name the player sees in the contract UI.

params.name: at
params.desc: The destination, as {x, y, z}. Use Ess.Easy.Debug.overlay() in game to read real coordinates off the screen.

params.name: radius
params.desc: How close the player has to get, in world units. Default 15.

params.name: tOpts
params.desc: Extras: desc (the objective line the player reads; defaults to the title) and reward = { cash = , fuel = }.

returns.name: id
returns.desc: The auto-generated contract id (easy1, easy2, ...) - keep it if you want to look this contract up later.

nodes.title: Easy Debug: Hide Overlay
