nodes.desc: Tints an area of the PDA's big map - the counterpart to the shaded region the radar nodes draw on the minimap. Use it for territory, a no-go zone or a search area. It shades a 'line region' that the level already defines and refers to it by handle, so this colours an existing shape in, it cannot invent one.
nodes.desc_short: Tints an area of the PDA's big map - the counterpart to the shaded region the radar nodes draw on the minimap.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The line region to shade, wired in as a live handle (a handle is the engine's own reference to a thing, not a name you type). Leave it empty and this node refuses the call rather than shading nothing.

params.name: tOpts
params.desc: How to colour it. rgb is a list of three channels, each 0-255. nAlpha is ALSO 0-255 like the others, not a percentage - the engine converts it to one internally, so passing something like 50 gives you a nearly invisible tint rather than half transparency. Leave both out and you get the game's own muted blue at 64/64/160, alpha 128. bInvert = true forwards the engine's invert flag; what exactly it flips is not documented, so treat it as something to try rather than rely on.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True once the shading was handed to the PDA. False only when no region handle was given.

nodes.title: PDA: Remove Map Blip
nodes.desc: Takes a blip back off the PDA map, by the name it was created with. Nothing removes blips automatically - not the end of a mission, not the thing they were attached to dying - so this (or a tracker) is what stops one sitting on the map for the rest of the session. The one exception is a blip that belongs to a mission: PDA: Remove Mission sweeps those up by itself.
nodes.desc_short: Takes a blip back off the PDA map, by the name it was created with.

params.name: sName
params.desc: The exact name you gave the blip when you added it. A name that was never used simply does nothing. Cannot be blank.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True once the removal was handed to the PDA. False only when the name was left blank.

nodes.title: PDA: Remove Mission
nodes.desc: Deletes a mission from the PDA and, at the same time, every blip that belonged to it - that cascade is the engine's own doing, so a finished mission needs no separate blip cleanup. If this was the mission the player had tracked, the tracking is cleared too.
nodes.desc_short: Deletes a mission from the PDA and, at the same time, every blip that belonged to it - that cascade is the...

params.name: sName
params.desc: The mission id to remove - the private name, not the label the player sees. Cannot be blank.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True once the removal was handed to the PDA. False only when the name was left blank.

nodes.title: PDA: Remove Map Region
nodes.desc: Clears the tint from an area you shaded with PDA: Shade Map Region, leaving that part of the map plain again. Give it the same region handle you shaded.
nodes.desc_short: Clears the tint from an area you shaded with PDA: Shade Map Region, leaving that part of the map plain again.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The line region whose shading to remove - the same handle you passed to PDA: Shade Map Region. Leave it empty and this node refuses the call.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True once the removal was handed to the PDA. False only when no region handle was given.

nodes.title: PDA: Track Mission
nodes.desc: Sets which mission the player is tracking, exactly as if they had picked it in the PDA themselves. Leave the socket empty to clear the tracking. Watch out: a name that is not a registered mission does not complain - it CLEARS the selection, which is the engine's behaviour and an easy way to believe a call worked when it did nothing.
nodes.desc_short: Sets which mission the player is tracking, exactly as if they had picked it in the PDA themselves.

params.name: sName
params.desc: The mission id to start tracking. Leave it empty to stop tracking anything. A misspelt name silently clears the tracking instead of erroring, so check it against PDA: Mission Exists if a track never seems to take.

nodes.title: PDA: Selected Mission
nodes.desc: Reads which mission the player currently has tracked in their PDA - one of the very few things in this whole area you can read back rather than only set. It always asks about the local player; there is no player-number option. Gives back nothing when no mission is selected.
nodes.desc_short: Reads which mission the player currently has tracked in their PDA - one of the very few things in this whole...

returns.name: sName
returns.desc: The tracked mission's id - the name it was registered under, not its on-screen label. Nil when the player has nothing selected.

nodes.title: PDA: Add Statistic Row
nodes.desc: Adds one 'label on the left, value on the right' row under a statistics heading - kills, distance driven, money earned, whatever your mod counts. Make the heading first with PDA: Add Statistics Category, or the row has nothing to attach to. Like categories, rows are add-only: there is no remove.
nodes.desc_short: Adds one 'label on the left, value on the right' row under a statistics heading - kills, distance driven,...

params.name: sCategory
params.desc: Which heading this row belongs under - the exact same text you gave PDA: Add Statistics Category. Cannot be blank.

params.name: sDesc
params.desc: The label down the left of the row - what is being counted. Anything you pass is turned into text; omit it and the label is blank.

params.name: sData
params.desc: The value shown on the right. It is displayed as text, so '7', '2:15' and '84%' are all fine - a number gets converted for you.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True once the row was handed to the PDA. False only when the category name was left blank.

nodes.title: PDA: Add Statistics Category
nodes.desc: Creates a heading on the PDA's statistics screen. The category has to exist BEFORE you add any rows to it - a row aimed at a heading that was never made has nowhere to go. Headings are add-only: there is no way to take one back off again.
nodes.desc_short: Creates a heading on the PDA's statistics screen.

params.name: sCategory
params.desc: The heading's name. This exact text is what you feed to PDA: Add Statistic Row to file rows underneath it, so keep the two spellings identical. Cannot be blank.

params.name: sIcon
params.desc: Optional picture shown next to the heading. Leave it empty for none.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True once the heading was handed to the PDA. False only when the category name was left blank.

nodes.title: PDA: Hide PDA
nodes.desc: Hides the whole PDA, or gives it back. The game uses this for briefings and cutscenes, where the player pulling up their map mid-scene would look wrong. Remember to switch it back on - a suppressed PDA stays suppressed until something turns it off.
nodes.desc_short: Hides the whole PDA, or gives it back.

params.name: bOn
params.desc: True hides the PDA entirely, false gives the player access to it again.

nodes.title: PDA: Set Mission Trackable
nodes.desc: Turns a mission's 'the player may track this' flag on or off. This is the working way to do it: the engine's own update-mission call is broken by a parameter mix-up that writes your true/false into the mission's SORT ORDER and leaves the flag untouched, so changing it any other way silently fails. A suppressed mission is forced untrackable by the game regardless of what you pass here.
nodes.desc_short: Turns a mission's 'the player may track this' flag on or off.

params.name: sName
params.desc: The mission id to change. Cannot be blank.

params.name: bOn
params.desc: True lets the player track this mission, false takes it off the list of things they can track.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True once the change was handed to the PDA. False only when the mission name was left blank.

nodes.title: Player: Camera
nodes.desc: Gets the camera handle belonging to a player in one step, instead of the usual two-step of fetching the player slot and then asking it for its camera.
nodes.desc_short: Gets the camera handle belonging to a player in one step, instead of the usual two-step of fetching the...

params.name: i
params.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner and has no camera in single-player.

returns.name: uCamera
returns.desc: The camera handle to hand to camera nodes, or nil if that player index has no slot.

nodes.title: Player: Cash
nodes.desc: Reads how much money the player has right now, so you can price something, refuse a purchase they cannot afford, or show a balance. This only READS - use Player: Give Cash to change it, and never the raw engine cash setter, which moves the number without refreshing the HUD so the player never sees it change. There is no player index because the wallet belongs to the session, not to a character; in co-op each machine has its own.
nodes.desc_short: Reads how much money the player has right now, so you can price something, refuse a purchase they cannot...

returns.name: n
returns.desc: The current cash amount, in whole dollars. Nil if the game could not be asked.

nodes.title: Player: Character
nodes.desc: Gets the handle for a player's actual body in the world - the thing you feed into almost every other node that acts on a person.
nodes.desc_short: Gets the handle for a player's actual body in the world - the thing you feed into almost every other node...

params.name: i
params.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, the local player. 1 is the co-op partner, and that is genuinely nil in single-player, so downstream nodes will do nothing.

returns.name: uChar
returns.desc: The character handle, or nil when there is no such player (index 1 outside co-op).

nodes.title: Player: Player Count
nodes.desc: How many player slots are actually filled in this session - 1 in single-player, 2 in co-op. Use it to size a loop over players, or to decide up front whether your mod needs to handle a partner at all. If the game cannot be asked it answers 1, so the single-player path is always the safe default.
nodes.desc_short: How many player slots are actually filled in this session - 1 in single-player, 2 in co-op.

returns.name: n
returns.desc: Number of players in the session. Remember player indexes count from ZERO, so a count of 2 means slots 0 and 1.

nodes.title: Player: Fuel
nodes.desc: Reads the player's fuel, handing back both how much they have and how much the tank holds. You get both because 'is it full' and 'how low am I' are the two things anyone actually asks, and the capacity is NOT a fixed number - it changes with saves and upgrades, so never hard-code it. Measured 300 out of 300 on a loaded save.
nodes.desc_short: Reads the player's fuel, handing back both how much they have and how much the tank holds.

returns.name: nCurrent
returns.desc: Fuel the player has right now.

returns.name: nCapacity
returns.desc: The most the tank can hold. Divide current by this for a 'how full' fraction rather than comparing against a number you typed in.

nodes.promoted_from_getter: multi-value return cannot be spliced inline as an expression

nodes.title: Player: Give Cash
nodes.desc: Adds money to the player's wallet through the route that also refreshes the HUD - the plain engine cash setters change the number without the player ever seeing it move.
nodes.desc_short: Adds money to the player's wallet through the route that also refreshes the HUD - the plain engine cash...

params.name: n
params.desc: How much cash to add. Amounts are whole dollars; a negative number takes money away.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the call went through.

nodes.title: Player: Give Fuel
nodes.desc: Adds fuel to the player's stock through the HUD-updating route, the same reason the cash node exists.
nodes.desc_short: Adds fuel to the player's stock through the HUD-updating route, the same reason the cash node exists.

params.name: n
params.desc: How much fuel to add. There is no player index here because fuel is this machine's own campaign stock, not a per-character resource - in co-op each machine already has its own.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the call went through.

nodes.title: Player: Vehicle They Are In
nodes.desc: Gets the vehicle the player is currently sitting in, driving or riding, so you can gate a boost, a horn or a car-only menu on actually being in one.
nodes.desc_short: Gets the vehicle the player is currently sitting in, driving or riding, so you can gate a boost, a horn or a...

params.name: i
params.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner.

returns.name: uVeh
returns.desc: The vehicle handle - driver OR passenger seat both count - or nil when they are on foot.

nodes.title: Player: Is Co-op
nodes.desc: Yes/no: is this genuinely a co-op session with another person in it? This is the honest check, and it matters because the tempting alternative lies - asking the engine for the second player SLOT hands back a real-looking handle even in single-player, so testing 'does slot 1 exist' says co-op when nobody is there. Use this node, or check whether the co-op partner has a character.
nodes.desc_short: Yes/no: is this genuinely a co-op session with another person in it?

returns.name: bCoop
returns.desc: True only in a real co-op session. Always plain true/false.

nodes.title: Player: Has Slot Joined
nodes.desc: Yes/no: is a given player slot actually occupied by someone? This node exists purely to defuse a nasty trap. The raw engine call wants a slot NUMBER, while nearly every other player call in this game wants a player handle - and if you hand it a handle it does not complain, it quietly answers 'no' forever, which looks like perfectly correct code that simply never fires. Measured live: slot 0 is true, slot 1 is false in single-player, and a handle gives nothing at all.
nodes.desc_short: Yes/no: is a given player slot actually occupied by someone?

params.name: i
params.desc: Which player slot, counting from ZERO: 0 (or blank) is you, the local player, and 1 is the co-op partner. Type a number here - do NOT wire a player handle in, which is exactly the mistake this node protects you from. Anything that is not 1 is treated as 0.

returns.name: bJoined
returns.desc: True when someone is really in that slot. Note that the engine will hand you a real-looking slot handle for an empty slot, so this - not 'does a slot handle exist' - is the trustworthy test.

nodes.title: Player: Profile Name
nodes.desc: Reads the profile name attached to a player slot - 'player0' on a plain local single-player save. Use it to address the player by name in your own messages, or to label who is who on screen in co-op.
nodes.desc_short: Reads the profile name attached to a player slot - 'player0' on a plain local single-player save.

params.name: i
params.desc: Which player, counting from ZERO: 0 (or blank) is you, the local player, and 1 is the co-op partner.

returns.name: sName
returns.desc: The slot's profile name, or nil if that slot has no player.

nodes.title: Player: Is On Foot
nodes.desc: The plain yes/no complement of the vehicle check - true when the player is in no vehicle at all.
nodes.desc_short: The plain yes/no complement of the vehicle check - true when the player is in no vehicle at all.

params.name: i
params.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner.

returns.name: bOnFoot
returns.desc: True when they are walking, false when they are in any vehicle.

nodes.title: Player: Pose
nodes.desc: One read that answers 'where is this player and which way are they turned', handing back the position, facing and both handles together so you do not need four separate nodes.
nodes.desc_short: One read that answers 'where is this player and which way are they turned', handing back the position, facing...

params.name: i
params.desc: Which player: 0 (or blank) is you, 1 is the co-op partner and returns nils for position in single-player.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: East/west world coordinate. Nil when there is no character at all.

returns.name: y
returns.desc: Height. Y is up on this engine.

nodes.title: Player: Point Ahead Of View
nodes.desc: Gives you a spot in the world out in front of where the player is LOOKING, taken straight from the camera - so it always works, with no need for the crosshair to be aimed at anything. Two measured traps. The distance is counted from the CAMERA, which sits about 3 units BEHIND the player, so the point lands a flat 3 units short of the number you type at every range (ask 25, get 22; ask 1600, get 1597). nodes.title: Quest: Step Sequence
nodes.desc: The middle weight: a linear sequence of goals, shown one at a time on the HUD objective line as '(2/3) Blow the tower'. Steps can be MANUAL (a plain line of text you advance yourself) or AUTO-WIRED - a reach, destroy or clear step completes itself off what actually happens in the world AND drops its own map marker, so a whole scripted mission becomes one table with no event wiring at all. When the last step is done the line clears and your completion callback fires. Heavier than a single Objective, far lighter than a Contract (no rewards, no spawned units, no fail conditions).
nodes.desc_short: The middle weight: a linear sequence of goals, shown one at a time on the HUD objective line as '(2/3) Blow...

params.name: opts
params.default: { steps = { { reach = { -522, -2.1, 2697, 10 }, label = 'Get to the docks' }, { clear = { -522, -2.1, 2697, 50, 'VZ' }, label = 'Clear them out' }, 'Escape on foot' }, onComplete = function() Ess.Easy.Toast('Mission complete!') end }
params.desc: The sequence spec. `steps` is the ordered list; each step is either `'plain text'` (manual - you call `:advance()`), `{label = , target = }` (a manual counted step), or one of the auto-wired kinds: `{reach = {x, y, z, radius}}` completes on arrival, `{destroy = guid}` when that object dies, `{clear = {x, y, z, radius, faction}}` when every unit of that faction in the area is dead. `onStep(i, total)` fires as each one clears, `onComplete` at the end. `showCounter = false` drops the '(2/3)' prefix.

returns.name: quest
returns.desc: The live sequence. Call `:advance(n)` to push the current step along, `:skip()` to force it done and move on, `:step()` for the current index and total, `:current()` for the live Objective, `:isDone()`, or `:cancel()` to abandon it.

nodes.title: Random: Chance
nodes.desc: Rolls against a probability and answers true or false - "does this enemy drop loot?", "does a car spawn here?". p runs 0 to 1, so 0.25 means it happens about a quarter of the time; leave it out for a straight coin flip. This is the engine-safe generator: use it, never Lua's math.random, which does not work in this game. Draws from a generator made by Random: New Generator.

nodes.desc_short: Rolls a whole number from 1 up to n - a dice roll, or a random slot in a list of n things.

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.RNG to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: n
params.desc: The highest number you can roll (the lowest is always 1).

returns.name: value
returns.desc: A whole number between 1 and n.

nodes.title: Random: New Generator
nodes.desc: Makes a random number generator that actually works in this game. Mercenaries 2's Lua stores numbers as 32-bit floats, so the usual random generators quietly break here - one real mod had every crate and unit roll come out identical for a whole play session before anyone noticed - and the engine's own math.random is dead too. Always start from this instead. Give it a seed number to get the same sequence every run (handy while testing), or leave it blank to seed from the clock. Each generator is its own independent stream, so two mods rolling in the same tick can't disturb each other.
nodes.desc_short: Makes a random number generator that actually works in this game.

params.name: seed
params.desc: A starting number for a repeatable sequence. Leave empty for a different sequence each run.

returns.name: generator
returns.desc: The generator to feed into the other Random nodes.

nodes.title: Random: Fraction
nodes.desc: Draws the next random fraction, from 0 up to (but never quite reaching) 1 - the raw roll every other Random node is built on. Multiply it to get any range you like. This is the engine-safe generator: use it, never Lua's math.random, which does not work in this game. Draws from a generator made by Random: New Generator.
nodes.desc_short: Draws the next random fraction, from 0 up to (but never quite reaching) 1 - the raw roll every other Random...

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.RNG to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: A random fraction from 0 up to just under 1.

nodes.title: Random: Pick One
nodes.desc: Picks one random entry out of a list, optionally weighted so some come up more often. If an entry is a table, its "w" field (or whichever key name you give) is how heavily it's weighted; plain entries like object handles, numbers or text all weigh 1, giving an even pick. This is the engine-safe generator: use it, never Lua's math.random, which does not work in this game. Draws from a generator made by Random: New Generator.
nodes.desc_short: Picks one random entry out of a list, optionally weighted so some come up more often.

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.RNG to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: list
params.desc: The list to pick from. Entries can be plain values, or tables carrying a weight.

params.name: weightKey
params.desc: Which field on a table entry holds its weight. Entries missing it weigh 1.

returns.name: picked
returns.desc: One entry from the list.

nodes.title: Random: Pick Several
nodes.desc: Picks n DIFFERENT entries from a list at random, in random order - a loot draw or a random squad selection where nothing repeats. Asking for more than the list holds just gives you all of it, shuffled; asking for none gives an empty list. Your original list is never touched. This is the engine-safe generator: use it, never Lua's math.random, which does not work in this game. Draws from a generator made by Random: New Generator.
nodes.desc_short: Picks n DIFFERENT entries from a list at random, in random order - a loot draw or a random squad selection...

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.RNG to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: list
params.desc: The list to draw from. Left unchanged.

params.name: n
params.desc: How many distinct entries you want.

returns.name: picked
returns.desc: A new list of n different entries, in random order.

nodes.title: Random: Shuffle List
nodes.desc: Shuffles a list into a random order. It rearranges the list you hand it (and gives that same list back), so copy it first if you need the original order kept. Use this rather than sorting with a random comparator - that trick is biased and can even crash, because an inconsistent comparator is undefined behaviour in Lua. This is the engine-safe generator: use it, never Lua's math.random, which does not work in this game. Draws from a generator made by Random: New Generator.
nodes.desc_short: Shuffles a list into a random order.

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.RNG to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: list
params.desc: The list to shuffle. It is rearranged in place.

returns.name: list
returns.desc: The same list, now in random order.

nodes.title: Raw AI: Freeze AI Control
nodes.desc: Turns the AI's control of a character on or off. Off freezes them exactly where they stand - the standard way to hold someone still for a scripted or cutscene beat - and on hands control back. Point it at a person; for someone in a vehicle, aim it at the driver rather than the vehicle.
nodes.desc_short: Turns the AI's control of a character on or off.

params.name: g
params.desc: The character to freeze or release.

params.name: bOn
params.desc: False freezes them (the AI stops driving them), true gives control back. Always pair the two - a frozen character stays frozen until something unfreezes them.

nodes.title: Raw AI: Make Enemies Focus This
nodes.desc: Marks one thing as the priority target for hostile AI, so enemies in the area come for it. This is the standalone 'everyone attack THIS' switch behind a boss fight or an escort-and-defend scenario, without having to hand orders to each enemy yourself.
nodes.desc_short: Marks one thing as the priority target for hostile AI, so enemies in the area come for it.

params.name: g
params.desc: The thing enemies should focus on - a player, an ally you want them to swarm, a vehicle.

nodes.title: Raw Mark: Blink Radar Dot
nodes.desc: Fades a radar dot that ALREADY EXISTS in and out, the quieter cousin of the throb. Like the other effects it only drives an existing dot by name - it never places one, and a name that matches nothing does nothing at all.
nodes.desc_short: Fades a radar dot that ALREADY EXISTS in and out, the quieter cousin of the throb.

params.name: sName
params.desc: The name of the dot to fade. Same name you gave Radar Dot At Point, or an object's text handle from the Name Of node if the dot was placed on an object.

params.name: tOpts
params.desc: The fade settings, all optional - leave it empty for the engine's own look. nDuration is how many seconds it runs, nMinAlpha and nMaxAlpha are how faint and how solid it gets (0 is invisible, 1 is fully solid), nSpeed is how fast. Set bOneWay = true to fade once instead of blinking on and on.

returns.name: bOk
returns.desc: True when the call went through without erroring - not a promise that a dot by that name was there to fade.

nodes.title: Raw Mark: Stop Flashing
nodes.desc: Stops the flashing that Raw Mark: Flash Marker started, leaving the marker itself in place. Like its partner it takes the object, not a marker handle.
nodes.desc_short: Stops the flashing that Raw Mark: Flash Marker started, leaving the marker itself in place.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The object that is currently flashing.

nodes.title: Raw Mark: Flash Marker
nodes.desc: Makes an object's EXISTING marker flash in a colour - a 'look at this' pulse, not a new marker. If the thing has no marker yet nothing will show, so place one with a Mark node first. Unlike the other marker calls, this one takes the object itself rather than a marker handle.
nodes.desc_short: Makes an object's EXISTING marker flash in a colour - a 'look at this' pulse, not a new marker.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The object whose marker should flash.

params.name: rgb
params.desc: Flash colour as { red, green, blue }, each 0 to 255. Left alone it is the game's own amber objective colour.

nodes.title: Raw Mark: Throb Radar Dot
nodes.desc: Makes a radar dot that ALREADY EXISTS grow and shrink over and over, so the eye is pulled to it. This does not create anything - if no dot with that name is on the radar, nothing happens and nothing warns you. Different from Flash Marker, which colours the icon floating in the world; this one throbs the minimap dot.
nodes.desc_short: Makes a radar dot that ALREADY EXISTS grow and shrink over and over, so the eye is pulled to it.

params.name: sName
params.desc: The name of the dot to animate. For a dot from Radar Dot At Point it is the name you invented; for a dot placed on an object it is that object's text handle, which the Name Of node gives you. Spelling must match exactly.

params.name: tOpts
params.desc: The throb settings, all optional - leave the whole thing empty for the engine's own look. nDuration is how many seconds it runs, nMin and nMax are the small and large sizes it swings between, nSpeed is how fast. Set bOneWay = true to grow once and stay big instead of swelling in and out.

returns.name: bOk
returns.desc: True when the call went through without erroring. It does NOT promise a dot by that name existed - a name that matches nothing still reports true.

nodes.title: Raw Mark: Radar Dot At Point
nodes.desc: Puts a dot on the minimap radar at a fixed spot in the world, with no object underneath it - the way to mark a PLACE rather than a THING (a stash location, a rendezvous, the corner you want people to gather at). The name you give it is how you find this dot again later: every other radar node - pulse, blink, sonar, stop, remove - takes that same name back.
nodes.desc_short: Puts a dot on the minimap radar at a fixed spot in the world, with no object underneath it - the way to mark...

params.name: sName
params.desc: A label you invent for this dot, and the ONLY way to reach it afterwards, so keep it and reuse it exactly. It must not be blank - a blank or non-text name is refused and no dot appears. Reusing a name that is already on the radar overwrites that dot.

params.name: x
params.desc: East/west world coordinate of the spot. Usually wired in from a Player Pose node while you are standing where you want the dot.

params.name: y
params.desc: Height of the spot. Worth filling in even though the radar is flat: leave it empty and the engine quietly uses 2, not 0.

params.name: z
params.desc: North/south world coordinate of the spot.

params.name: tex
params.desc: Which radar icon to draw. Real ones that work: "objective_action" (the amber default), "objective_destroy", "objective_defend", "objective_verify", "objective_outpost", "objective_deliverable". An icon name that does not exist simply draws nothing rather than complaining.

params.name: rgb
params.desc: Colour of the dot as { red, green, blue }, each 0 to 255. Left alone it is the game's own amber objective colour.

returns.name: sName
returns.desc: The same name back, or nothing at all if the dot could not be placed. Hold on to it - it is what the pulse, blink, sonar, stop and remove nodes need.

nodes.title: Raw Mark: Shade Map Region
nodes.desc: Tints a whole area of the minimap in a colour, instead of dropping a dot on it - this is the effect the base game uses to show faction territory boundaries. Good for 'this district is hostile' or 'stay inside this zone'. It is drawn by a different part of the HUD from every other radar node here, so the throb, blink and sonar effects do not apply to it and Remove Radar will not clear it - use Unshade Map Region.
nodes.desc_short: Tints a whole area of the minimap in a colour, instead of dropping a dot on it - this is the effect the base...

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The live handle of the region whose shape gets shaded - a zone or territory the level already has, looked up by name with a Find By Name node. This is the one node here keyed to an object handle rather than a dot name, and the same handle is what Unshade Map Region needs later.

params.name: rgb
params.desc: Shading colour as { red, green, blue }, each 0 to 255. Both of the base game's own uses are plain black, which reads as 'darkened out' rather than as a colour.

params.name: nAlpha
params.desc: How heavy the shading is, from 0 (nothing) to 255 (solid). The game's own two uses both pick 160, a strong tint you can still see the map through.

params.name: bInvert
params.desc: False shades INSIDE the region. True flips it and shades everything OUTSIDE instead, which is how you say 'only this patch matters' by dimming the rest of the map.

returns.name: bOk
returns.desc: True when the call went through without erroring.

nodes.title: Raw Mark: Unshade Map Region
nodes.desc: Clears the minimap shading put down by Shade Map Region, returning that area to normal. It takes the region's handle, not a dot name, and it is the only node that removes this - Remove Radar deals with dots and will not touch a shaded region.
nodes.desc_short: Clears the minimap shading put down by Shade Map Region, returning that area to normal.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The same region handle you passed to Shade Map Region. A different handle just clears nothing.

returns.name: bOk
returns.desc: True when the call went through without erroring.

nodes.title: Raw Mark: Show Player Markers
nodes.desc: One global switch for whether the other players' HUD markers draw at all. The confirmed use is quieting the HUD for a scripted moment: turn it off as your cutscene starts, back on when it ends. Unlike every other marker call this is not tied to a single object - it affects all of them at once, so always turn it back on.
nodes.desc_short: One global switch for whether the other players' HUD markers draw at all.

params.name: bOn
params.desc: True draws player markers, false hides them.

nodes.title: Raw Mark: Sonar Sweep
nodes.desc: The expanding-ring sonar ping around a radar dot that ALREADY EXISTS - the showiest effect the radar has, and the one the base game uses to say 'something is happening over here'. Rings grow outward and fade, one after another. It drives an existing dot by name and never places one.
nodes.desc_short: The expanding-ring sonar ping around a radar dot that ALREADY EXISTS - the showiest effect the radar has, and...

params.name: sName
params.desc: The name of the dot to sweep from. The name you invented with Radar Dot At Point, or an object's text handle from the Name Of node.

params.name: tOpts
params.desc: The sweep settings, all optional. nDuration is seconds, and 0 means keep going forever until you stop it. nTotalBlips is how many rings are in the cycle and nVisibleBlips how many show at once; nMinWidth and nMaxWidth are the ring sizes it grows between; nBlipDelay is the gap between rings; nAlphaAtMin and nAlphaAtMax how solid a ring is when small and when large; nGrowSpeed how fast; rgb is { red, green, blue }, 0 to 255 each. sTexture picks the ring picture and already defaults to the game's own "temp_radar_pulse".

returns.name: bOk
returns.desc: True when the call went through without erroring - not a promise that a dot by that name was there to sweep.

nodes.title: Raw Mark: Stop Radar Effect
nodes.desc: Calms a radar dot back down, ending the throb, blink or sonar sweep running on it. The dot itself stays on the radar - use Remove Radar to take the dot away. You need this for any sonar sweep left running with nDuration 0, since that one never stops on its own.
nodes.desc_short: Calms a radar dot back down, ending the throb, blink or sonar sweep running on it.

params.name: sName
params.desc: The name of the dot to calm down - the same name you animated.

params.name: sType
params.desc: Which effect to end. LEAVE THIS ALONE: "all" is the only value anyone has confirmed works, and it stops everything at once. The per-effect names are decided deep inside the game where nobody can read them, so "size", "alpha" or "sonar" may simply be ignored - and being ignored looks exactly like nothing happening.

returns.name: bOk
returns.desc: True when the call went through without erroring.

nodes.title: Relations: Apply Faction Stances
nodes.desc: Sets how whole factions feel about each other - who shoots at whom - and hands back a handle that undoes it. This is how you make a normally peaceful faction turn on the player for your fight. Both directions are set at once, so making China hate PMC also makes PMC hate China. TRAP: this is a real change to the world and it does not wear off on its own. If you never restore the handle, those factions stay at each other for the rest of the session.
nodes.desc_short: Sets how whole factions feel about each other - who shoots at whom - and hands back a handle that undoes it.

params.name: pairsList
params.desc: The stances to set, as a list of {faction, faction, stance} entries. Faction names the game knows: Allied, China, Guerilla, OC, Pirate, VZ, PMC. Stance is 'friend', 'ally', 'allied', 'neutral', 'enemy' or 'hostile' (any capitalisation), or a raw number from -100 for hatred to 100 for friendship. A faction name this level does not know is written to the log and skipped, so a typo changes nothing at all. A pair involving PMC also updates the other faction's attitude on the HUD so the player can see the change.

params.name: label
params.desc: A name for this set of changes. Only used to make the log readable when several sets are live at once.

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: Keep this. Feed it to the Relations: Restore node (or an Ess.stop node) when the fight is over, or your stance change stays live for the whole session. Each apply mints its own handle carrying its own before-picture, so several sets can be live at the same time without overwriting each other.

nodes.title: Relations: Get Personal Feeling
nodes.desc: Reads how one specific character feels about one other specific character. This is a personal grudge between two individuals, which is a completely different thing from the faction-wide stances the Relations: Apply node sets - you can make one guard friendly without touching his whole army.
nodes.desc_short: Reads how one specific character feels about one other specific character.

params.name: uGuidA
params.desc: The character whose opinion you are reading.

params.name: uGuidB
params.desc: The character they have an opinion about.

returns.name: feeling
returns.desc: Roughly -100 for wants-you-dead up to 100 for friendly; below zero is hostile. Two catches: a failed read also comes back as 0, so 0 means 'neutral, or could not tell', and a character you spawned this very instant reads back a stale 0 - wait a tick before asking about anything freshly spawned.

nodes.title: Relations: Get Detectability
nodes.desc: Reads how visible a character is to enemy AI - the stealth stat behind sneaking past people. Live readings taken from the running game: 90 with a floor of 5 on a person on foot, 90 with a floor of 2.5 on a helicopter pilot.
nodes.desc_short: Reads how visible a character is to enemy AI - the stealth stat behind sneaking past people.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The character to measure. Anything spawned this instant needs a tick to settle before it reads back correctly.

returns.name: n
returns.desc: How detectable this character currently is. Nothing comes back at all if the read failed.

returns.name: floor
returns.desc: The engine's lower limit for this character - the most hidden it will let them get.

nodes.promoted_from_getter: multi-value return cannot be spliced inline as an expression

nodes.title: Relations: Is Set Still Applied
nodes.desc: Checks whether a set of faction stance changes is still in force, so you can avoid restoring twice or show the player that a truce is still running.
nodes.desc_short: Checks whether a set of faction stance changes is still in force, so you can avoid restoring twice or show...

params.name: h
params.desc: The handle the Relations: Apply node gave you.

returns.name: active
returns.desc: True while this handle's stances are still applied, false once it has been restored.

nodes.title: Relations: Restore Faction Stances
nodes.desc: Puts back exactly the faction stances that one apply changed, and nothing else. This is the other half of Relations: Apply and the thing beginners forget - skip it and your world stays rewritten. Safe to run twice: a second go, or a blank handle, quietly does nothing.
nodes.desc_short: Puts back exactly the faction stances that one apply changed, and nothing else.

params.name: h
params.desc: The handle the Relations: Apply node gave you. If the original stance could not be read back when it was applied, there is genuinely nothing to restore it to, so that one direction is left as-is and written to the log rather than being silently skipped.

nodes.title: Relations: Set Personal Feeling
nodes.desc: Changes how one character feels about one other character, without touching either one's faction. The game's own recruit script does exactly this - writing 100 to clear a guard's hostility toward the player - immediately before giving that guard a follow order, because a hostile character refuses to follow anyone.
nodes.desc_short: Changes how one character feels about one other character, without touching either one's faction.

params.name: uGuidA
params.desc: The character whose opinion is being changed.

params.name: uGuidB
params.desc: The character they will now feel differently about. This is one-way only: A's opinion of B. Set the other direction too if you want it mutual.

params.name: n
params.desc: The new feeling, roughly -100 for hatred up to 100 for friendship. 100 is the value the game's own scripts use to wipe out hostility before a follow order.

nodes.title: Relations: Set Detectability
nodes.desc: Turns a character's visibility to enemy AI up or down - the knob behind a ghost or stealth mode. It is fully reversible: the value was driven from 90 down to 30 and back to 90 in a live session with clean reads in between. Honest caveat: the number provably moves, but whether AI genuinely stop noticing someone at a low value has not yet been proven in actual gameplay, so test your stealth mode rather than trusting the number.
nodes.desc_short: Turns a character's visibility to enemy AI up or down - the knob behind a ghost or stealth mode.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The character to make more or less noticeable.

params.name: n
params.desc: The new detectability. Typical starting value is 90, and the engine has its own floor per character (around 5 for a person on foot) that it will not go below. Remember the old value if you want to put it back.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the engine accepted the change.

nodes.title: Reset Failure Stats
nodes.desc: Wipes the failure tally, the running total and the last error, so whatever shows up afterwards came only from the thing you are about to do. The habit that makes the diagnostics readable: reset, reproduce your problem once, then read Last Error or Failure Stats.
nodes.desc_short: Wipes the failure tally, the running total and the last error, so whatever shows up afterwards came only from...

nodes.title: Failure Stats
nodes.desc: The worst-offenders list: which calls have been failing, and how often, sorted worst first. It only tallies failures that happened while debug was on (a Lua line reading Ess.DEBUG = true), while the running total counts them either way - so an empty list next to a big total means plenty failed, just before you started watching.
nodes.desc_short: The worst-offenders list: which calls have been failing, and how often, sorted worst first.

returns.name: byCall
returns.desc: A list of records with .label and .count, worst first. Empty unless debug was on when things failed.

returns.name: total
returns.desc: Every failure Ess has quietly swallowed this session, counted whether or not debug was on.

nodes.promoted_from_getter: multi-value return cannot be spliced inline as an expression

nodes.title: Sandbox: Begin
nodes.desc: Opens a temporary, guaranteed-cleanup mode for a fight: several parts of the world are photographed, changed for the duration, and put back by the matching Sandbox: Finish node. Saving is deliberately switched off the whole time, so if the game crashes in the middle of your encounter the save on disk is still the untouched pre-encounter one. TRAP: if you never finish this id, the player cannot save for the rest of the session.
nodes.desc_short: Opens a temporary, guaranteed-cleanup mode for a fight: several parts of the world are photographed, changed...

params.name: id
params.desc: A name for this sandbox. Pass the exact same name to Sandbox: Finish to close it. Two sandboxes can run at once as long as they have different names.

params.name: providerNames
params.desc: Which parts of the world to isolate, as a list of names. 'relations' applies the faction stances in opts.relations and puts them back at the end. 'economy' banks the player's cash to zero for the duration (or to opts.startCash) and pays back the exact amount afterwards. 'supports' empties the HUD support quick-select menu and restores the old items. 'layers' opens a layer mode under this same name. A misspelled provider name is logged and skipped rather than guessed at.

params.name: opts
params.desc: Settings the providers read: relations = the {faction, faction, stance} list for the relations provider, startCash = the wallet to hand the player for the duration for the economy provider.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the sandbox opened. False if a sandbox with this name is already open, or if every provider name was unknown or failed - in that case nothing was isolated and there is nothing to finish, so check your spelling rather than carrying on.

nodes.title: Sandbox: Finish
nodes.desc: Closes the sandbox with this name: every part of the world it isolated is restored in order, and this sandbox's hold on saving is released. Saving only truly comes back once every OTHER sandbox and every layer mode has also finished, so if the player still cannot save afterwards, something else is still open. Finishing a name that is not open does nothing.
nodes.desc_short: Closes the sandbox with this name: every part of the world it isolated is restored in order, and this...

params.name: id
params.desc: The same name you passed to Sandbox: Begin.

nodes.title: Sandbox: Is Active
nodes.desc: Checks whether a sandbox with this name is currently open, so you can avoid opening it twice or show the player that the mode is running.
nodes.desc_short: Checks whether a sandbox with this name is currently open, so you can avoid opening it twice or show the...

params.name: id
params.desc: The sandbox name to check.

returns.name: active
returns.desc: True while that sandbox is open.

nodes.title: Save: Block Saving
nodes.desc:
Stops the game writing a savegame or autosave while something temporary is going on, so the player cannot save mid-cutscene or mid-sandbox and be stuck with it forever.

It works by holders: saving stays blocked while at least ONE holder is active, and resumes only when the last one is gone. Blocking twice under the same name is still a single holder, so one unblock clears it. A world reload clears every holder, so a script that dies halfway cannot leave the player unable to save forever.
nodes.desc_short: Stops the game writing a savegame or autosave while something temporary is going on, so the player cannot...

params.name: sHolderKey
params.desc: A name only YOUR feature uses. If two features share a name they share one holder, so the first to unblock lets saving through while the other still believes it is blocked. Leaving it empty falls back to the shared name 'default', which is exactly the collision to avoid.

nodes.title: Save: Who Is Blocking
nodes.desc: The names of everything currently blocking saves. This is the diagnostic to reach for when the game has stopped saving and you want to know which feature forgot to clean up after itself.
nodes.desc_short: The names of everything currently blocking saves.

returns.name: holders
returns.desc: A plain list of holder names, empty when saving is allowed. Print it in a Lua field to see who is at fault.

nodes.title: Save: Is Blocked
nodes.desc: Is saving currently suppressed by anyone. Worth checking before telling the player something was saved.
nodes.desc_short: Is saving currently suppressed by anyone.

returns.name: gated
returns.desc: True while at least one holder is blocking saves.

nodes.title: Save: Allow Saving
nodes.desc: Removes your holder. Saving only actually resumes once the LAST holder is gone, so if something else is still blocking, this correctly leaves it blocked. Pair one of these with every Save: Block Saving.
nodes.desc_short: Removes your holder. Saving only actually resumes once the LAST holder is gone, so if something else is still...

params.name: sHolderKey
params.desc: The exact name you blocked with. A different name here removes nothing and leaves saving blocked - the usual cause of 'the game will not save any more'.

nodes.title: SaveVar: Get Saved Flag
nodes.desc:
Reads a saved yes/no that answers NO the first time, before it has ever been set - exactly the shape of 'has the player unlocked this yet', with the fresh-install answer already built in.

It is strict: only a real saved true reads as yes. That matters here, because in Lua a 0 counts as true and would otherwise fool a plain check.
nodes.desc_short: Reads a saved yes/no that answers NO the first time, before it has ever been set - exactly the shape of 'has...

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.SaveVar to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: key
params.desc: The name of the flag in your drawer. Same prefix, same key, or you are reading a different flag entirely.

returns.name: on
returns.desc: True only if a real true was saved under that key. Anything else, including never having been set, reads as false.

nodes.title: SaveVar: Get Saved Value
nodes.desc:
Reads a value back out of your mod's drawer in the game's saved-variable file. This is the storage that survives QUITTING the game, so it is where totals, unlocks and settings belong.

The prefix on the drawer is the whole point: it is what keeps your 'xp' separate from every other mod's 'xp'. Read with a different prefix and you are looking in somebody else's drawer, which is why the prefix must match everywhere you use it. Building a fresh drawer inline is otherwise harmless - two drawers with the same prefix are the same drawer.
nodes.desc_short: Reads a value back out of your mod's drawer in the game's saved-variable file.

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.SaveVar to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: key
params.desc: The name of the value inside your drawer. Stored as prefix_key behind the scenes, so it can never collide with another mod's key of the same name.

params.name: default
params.desc: What to hand back the very first time, before anything has ever been saved - 0, 'none', false. Without one you get nothing back on a fresh install and any sum you feed it breaks.

returns.name: value
returns.desc: The stored value, or your fallback if that key has never been written. Only numbers, text and yes/no values can live here - tables and object handles cannot be saved.

nodes.title: SaveVar: Namespace
nodes.desc:
Opens your mod's own private drawer in the game's saved-variable file - the only storage here that survives QUITTING the game, not just a re-run or a reload.

That file is one flat space shared by every mod, so this stamps your prefix onto every key and two mods can never tread on each other. Only numbers, text and yes/no values can be stored: no tables, no object handles.

Use it for unlocks, totals and settings. For 'my toggle keeps resetting' within a session, you want an Ess.State table instead - this one hits the disk.
nodes.desc_short: Opens your mod's own private drawer in the game's saved-variable file - the only storage here that survives...

params.name: prefix
params.desc: Your mod's name. Every key is stored as prefix_key, so pick something distinctive - two mods sharing a prefix will overwrite each other's saved values.

returns.name: sv
returns.desc: The drawer. Reading and writing are methods, so they have no nodes of their own - type them into any Lua field: sv:get('xp', 0) with a fallback for the first ever run, sv:set('xp', 5), sv:flag('unlocked') for a yes/no that defaults to no, and sv:setFlag('unlocked', true).

nodes.title: SaveVar: Set Saved Value
nodes.desc:
Writes a value into your mod's drawer, on disk. It is still there after the player quits the game entirely - that is the difference between this and an Ess.State table, which only survives your script re-running and is gone when the game closes.

Writing the same key again simply overwrites it. Keep writes sensible: this hits a file, so do not call it on every tick of a loop - save when something actually changes.
nodes.desc_short: Writes a value into your mod's drawer, on disk.

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.SaveVar to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: key
params.desc: The name to store it under, inside your prefixed drawer. Read it back with the same key and the same prefix.

params.name: value
params.desc: The value: a number, a piece of text in quotes, or true/false. Nothing else survives - a table or an object handle cannot be stored and will not come back.

nodes.title: SaveVar: Set Saved Flag
nodes.desc:
Stores a yes/no on disk, so it is still set after the player quits and comes back - the write half of 'this is unlocked now'.

It forces whatever you give it into a strict true or false before saving, so the value always reads back cleanly through SaveVar: Get Saved Flag.
nodes.desc_short: Stores a yes/no on disk, so it is still set after the player quits and comes back - the write half of 'this...

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.SaveVar to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: key
params.desc: The name of the flag in your drawer.

params.name: bOn
params.desc: On or off. Anything truthy is stored as a plain true and anything else as a plain false, so it can never come back as a surprising value.

nodes.title: Scroll Log: Create
nodes.desc: Build a scrolling text box -- the translucent dark chat-style panel -- needing no .gfx asset at all. TRAP: it starts HIDDEN and only appears once you add your first message to the returned handle (handle:add("text", seconds)). Second trap: messages QUEUE. Each one holds the box for its whole display time before the next can appear, which is why the per-message default is a deliberately short 1 second -- a long duration on a burst of lines can block the box for literally minutes. Calling this again with the same name hands back the SAME box instead of stacking a second one on top.
nodes.desc_short: Build a scrolling text box -- the translucent dark chat-style panel -- needing no .gfx asset at all.

params.name: name
params.desc: A name for this box. Reusing the name reuses the same box rather than making another.

params.name: x
params.desc: Left edge. Defaults to 20.

params.name: y
params.desc: Top edge. Defaults to 150.

params.name: w
params.desc: Width. Defaults to 340.

params.name: h
params.desc: Height. Defaults to 220.

returns.desc: The scroll-log handle -- call :add(msg, seconds), :setVisible(true/false) and :clearAll() on it. Nothing comes back if the box could not be built.
returns.name: result

nodes.title: Shop: Close Store
nodes.desc: Shuts the shop and, just as importantly, GIVES THE PLAYER THEIR CONTROLS BACK. Closing this shop with Escape was measured to leave the player unable to move at all: the game's own close never restores the control flag when nothing else is holding focus. So this node also un-sticks that flag, puts the HUD back and clears the leftover shell state. It is safe to call when no shop is open, and that is the whole point - it is the rescue for a stranded player as much as it is a close button.
nodes.desc_short: Shuts the shop and, just as importantly, GIVES THE PLAYER THEIR CONTROLS BACK.

nodes.title: Shop: Is Store Open
nodes.desc: Tells you whether a shop opened through this framework is currently on screen. Use it to avoid trying to open a second one, since the game refuses a second shop for the same player and a forgotten one blocks every later attempt. It follows the player closing the shop themselves as well as your own close.
nodes.desc_short: Tells you whether a shop opened through this framework is currently on screen.

returns.name: bOpen
returns.desc: True while the shop is showing, false once it has closed or if one was never opened.

nodes.title: Shop: Open Store
nodes.desc: Opens the game's REAL full-screen purchase screen - item tiles, icons, prices, a live cash readout, the whole storefront - stocked with items you invented, and calls you back when the player buys one. It runs the whole fiddly six-step setup in one go and quietly closes any shop left open beforehand, since the game refuses a second shop for the same player. Know that it is MODAL: it takes the controls and hides the HUD while it is up, and the player's three equipped support slots get added on top of your list, so your items are never the only things on the shelf.
nodes.desc_short: Opens the game's REAL full-screen purchase screen - item tiles, icons, prices, a live cash readout, the whole...

params.name: tItems
params.default: { { sName = "Ammo Crate", sDesc = "A crate of rifle ammunition.", sTexture = "supplies_PMC_crate", nCost = 500, nOwned = 0, nCap = 10 } }
params.desc: A Lua list of item tables. Every item MUST have sName, sDesc, sTexture and nCost - an item missing any of those is silently skipped, and if none survive the shop refuses to open. IMPORTANT: the optional nOwned and nCap are HOW MANY THE PLAYER ALREADY HAS and the most they may hold - they are the player's stockpile, NOT shelf stock. An item at nOwned = 0 is not sold out; the player owns none yet and can still buy up to nCap (default 99). Other optional fields: sId (the name reported back to onBuy - set it yourself if sName is translated), bUnlocked (true here by default, so the item can actually be bought), bNew, bFuelTank, nFuelQuantity. For sTexture, note an icon name the game cannot resolve draws a black box with an X instead of failing, so test yours - Ess.Shop.ICONS lists a dozen verified ones.

params.name: tOpts
params.default: { onBuy = function(sId, nQty) Ess.Log("bought " .. tostring(sId) .. " x" .. tostring(nQty)) end }
params.desc: Optional settings table carrying two callbacks. onBuy(sId, nQuantity) runs each time the player buys something, and tells you WHICH item and HOW MANY - it does not fire when they merely close the shop. onClose() runs when the shop goes away, however that happened. Leave the whole thing empty to just put the shop on screen and ignore what the player does.

returns.name: bOpened
returns.desc: True if the shop is on screen. False means it refused - an empty item list, no local player, or every item missing a required field. Switch on Ess.DEBUG to see which step gave up.

nodes.title: Sound: Start Ambience Loop
nodes.desc: Start a looping background ambience bed -- distant gunfire, jungle, city hum. Unlike a sound effect it keeps playing indefinitely, until you shut it off with Sound: Stop Ambience using the same stream name.
nodes.desc_short: Start a looping background ambience bed -- distant gunfire, jungle, city hum.

params.name: sStreamName
params.desc: The ambience stream name, e.g. "emt_distant_battle_01" (the game's own distant-battle bed) or "amb_jungle".

nodes.title: Sound: Category Pitch
nodes.desc: Reads the playback speed of one mixer group, where 1 is normal. Mainly there to confirm a pitch effect you applied actually landed - and remember an audio change is not visible to a read until the NEXT FRAME, so sample it a frame later, never in the same breath as the write.
nodes.desc_short: Reads the playback speed of one mixer group, where 1 is normal.

params.name: sCategory
params.desc: Which mixer group to read: "sfx", "music", "ambience" or "vo". Anything else quietly gives nothing back - this node does not complain about a bad name the way its siblings do.

returns.name: nPitch
returns.desc: 1 is normal speed, below 1 is slower and deeper, above 1 is faster and higher. Nothing comes back if the engine will not answer for that name.

nodes.title: Sound: Category Volume
nodes.desc: Reads how loud one of the four mixer groups - "sfx", "music", "ambience", "vo" - currently is, on a 0 to 1 scale. THE BIG TRAP: this gives the EFFECTIVE loudness, meaning the group's own level multiplied by its parent's, while Sound: Set Category Volume takes the group's OWN level - and "ambience" sits underneath "sfx". So never save a reading from here and write it back later to "restore" it: doing that leaves the group audibly quieter than it started. Remember the value you SET, or reset to 1.
nodes.desc_short: Reads how loud one of the four mixer groups - "sfx", "music", "ambience", "vo" - currently is, on a 0 to 1...

params.name: sCategory
params.desc: Which mixer group to read: "sfx", "music", "ambience" or "vo". "music" and "vo" stand alone, "ambience" is a child of "sfx" so pulling sfx down drags ambience with it.

returns.name: nVolume
returns.desc: The effective volume, 0 (silent) to 1 (full). Nothing comes back if the name is blank or the engine will not answer for it.

nodes.title: Sound: Clear Ducking
nodes.desc: The escape hatch for a mix that has got stuck quiet: it drops every stacked duck at once and puts every group's pitch back to normal, in one call, with nothing to fill in. Because ducks and pitch changes stack, an unbalanced mod can leave the game permanently muffled with no obvious way back - this is that way back. Worth wiring into your mod's cleanup as a matter of habit.
nodes.desc_short: The escape hatch for a mix that has got stuck quiet: it drops every stacked duck at once and puts every...

nodes.title: Sound: Play Sound
nodes.desc: Play a one-shot sound effect the player hears immediately. Leave the object empty for a plain UI/HUD beep with no position in the world -- the convention the game's own menu code uses. Give it a real object handle instead and the sound plays FROM that object, so it gets quieter as you walk away: an alarm on a building, an engine on a vehicle.
nodes.desc_short: Play a one-shot sound effect the player hears immediately.

params.name: uGuidOrNil
params.desc: Optional object for the sound to come from. Leave it empty for a plain UI sound with no world position.

params.name: sCueName
params.desc: The sound cue name, e.g. "ui_HUD_Objective_Complete" (objective chime), "ui_signal_ding_up" or "ui_HUD_Timer_Alert".

nodes.title: Sound: Duck Category
nodes.desc: Smoothly pulls one mixer group down to a quieter level - this is the game's own trick for dropping the music and gunfire underneath a line of dialogue, and it slides over a fade time rather than snapping. ALWAYS PAIR IT WITH Sound: Unduck Category. Ducks stack: each duck pushes one level and each unduck pops exactly one, so three ducks and one unduck leaves the group two levels down with no obvious way back. Sound: Clear Ducking is the way out of that.
nodes.desc_short: Smoothly pulls one mixer group down to a quieter level - this is the game's own trick for dropping the music...

params.name: sCategory
params.desc: Which mixer group to quieten: "sfx", "music", "ambience" or "vo". Remember "ambience" rides under "sfx", so ducking sfx quietens the ambience bed too.

params.name: nLevel
params.desc: How quiet to go, 0 (silent) to 1 (no change). Leave it empty for 0.2, which is well down but still audible.

params.name: nFade
params.desc: Seconds to slide down over. Leave it empty for half a second; 0 snaps immediately, which sounds abrupt.

returns.name: bOk
returns.desc: True if the request was accepted. False only means the category name was blank or not text.

nodes.title: Sound: Cue Length
nodes.desc: Asks how many seconds long a sound is - and, more usefully, whether the game can find that sound at all. A number above 0 is a real cue and its length; -1 means a real cue with NO fixed length, i.e. a loop; and nothing at all comes back when the engine cannot resolve the name. Careful with that last case: it means either you mistyped the name OR the sound is real but its bank is not loaded at this moment, so an empty answer means "cannot answer", not "does not exist".
nodes.desc_short: Asks how many seconds long a sound is - and, more usefully, whether the game can find that sound at all.

params.name: sCue
params.desc: The game's internal name for the sound, e.g. "fol_bldg_alarm_activate" (a real building alarm, measured with a proper length). Must not be blank - a blank name is refused and logged.

returns.name: nSeconds
returns.desc: Length in seconds for an ordinary sound, -1 for a loop that never ends by itself, or nothing at all if the engine cannot resolve the name right now.

nodes.title: Sound: Audio System Info
nodes.desc: One box that reports everything the audio system will admit about itself: the sound library version (12 on this build), the folder it streams audio out of, whether dynamic, faction-locked and action-locked music are switched on, and a live reading of all four mixer groups. It is a debugging node - take a snapshot before you start changing the mixer so you can see afterwards what actually moved.
nodes.desc_short: One box that reports everything the audio system will admit about itself: the sound library version (12 on...

returns.name: tInfo
returns.desc: A table holding nLibVersion, sAudioDir, bDynamicMusic, bFactionLocked and bActionLocked, plus one entry each for sfx, music, ambience and vo. Those four are EFFECTIVE volumes, so do not feed them straight back into Sound: Set Category Volume - that would leave the mix quieter than you found it.

nodes.title: Sound: Does This Cue Exist
nodes.desc: Checks whether the game can find this sound RIGHT NOW, before you try to play it. This is the single most useful node in the Sound group for a beginner, because a mistyped cue name is COMPLETELY SILENT - no error, no warning, no return value, nothing to tell you why your mod makes no noise. Use it as a guard whenever the cue name was typed by hand or built at runtime.
nodes.desc_short: Checks whether the game can find this sound RIGHT NOW, before you try to play it.

params.name: sCue
params.desc: The sound cue name you are about to play, e.g. "fol_bldg_alarm_activate" or "ui_HUD_Objective_Complete".

returns.name: bExists
returns.desc: True if the sound can be played this instant. A false is NOT proof of a typo - a real sound whose bank has not streamed in yet also reads false, so treat it as "cannot play it now".

nodes.title: Sound: Is This Cue A Loop
nodes.desc: Tells you whether a sound runs forever instead of stopping on its own - an alarm, an engine hum, a siren. Worth checking before you play something you had not planned to switch off, because a loop keeps going until Sound: Stop Sound is called with the SAME object and the SAME cue name you started it with.
nodes.desc_short: Tells you whether a sound runs forever instead of stopping on its own - an alarm, an engine hum, a siren.

params.name: sCue
params.desc: The sound cue name to test, e.g. "fol_alarm_bldg_01" (a building alarm loop, measured as endless).

returns.name: bLooping
returns.desc: True only for a sound with no fixed length. A name the engine cannot resolve also gives false, so pair this with Sound: Does This Cue Exist if you need to tell the two apart.

nodes.title: Sound: Set Category Pitch
nodes.desc: Speeds up or slows down everything in one mixer group, which also drags its pitch with it - the obvious use is a slow-motion or drugged feel on "sfx". As with volume, the write does not show up on a read until the next frame. If you lose track of what you have applied, Sound: Clear Ducking puts every group's pitch back to normal in one call.
nodes.desc_short: Speeds up or slows down everything in one mixer group, which also drags its pitch with it - the obvious use...

params.name: sCategory
params.desc: Which mixer group to change: "sfx", "music", "ambience" or "vo".

params.name: nPitch
params.desc: The speed multiplier. 1 is normal, 0.5 is half speed and an octave down, 1.5 is faster and higher.

returns.name: bOk
returns.desc: True if the request was accepted. False means a blank category or a pitch that was not a number, and the reason was logged.

nodes.title: Sound: Set Category Volume
nodes.desc: Turns one mixer group up or down - the way to quieten all the music without touching gunfire. You are setting that group's OWN level, 0 to 1. Two things will confuse you otherwise: reading it back afterwards gives own level times parent rather than the number you typed ("ambience" lives under "sfx"), and the change is NOT VISIBLE TO A READ UNTIL THE NEXT FRAME - checking in the same breath always shows the old value and makes a working write look broken. To undo, set 1 rather than restoring a number you read earlier.
nodes.desc_short: Turns one mixer group up or down - the way to quieten all the music without touching gunfire.

params.name: sCategory
params.desc: Which mixer group to change: "sfx", "music", "ambience" or "vo".

params.name: nLevel
params.desc: The group's own level: 0 is silent, 1 is full. Note the game's own defaults are around 0.75 for each of these, so 1 here is slightly LOUDER than a fresh install, not the same.

returns.name: bOk
returns.desc: True if the request was accepted. False means the input was wrong - a blank category or a level that was not a number - and the reason was logged. It does not promise anything is audibly different.

nodes.title: Sound: Stop Sound
nodes.desc: Stop a sound started with Sound: Play Sound. TRAP: you must pass the SAME object and the SAME cue name you started it with, or nothing stops. Mostly useful for looping cues -- a one-shot effect ends on its own anyway.
nodes.desc_short: Stop a sound started with Sound: Play Sound.

params.name: uGuidOrNil
params.desc: The same object you played it from. Leave empty if you played it as a plain UI sound.

params.name: sCueName
params.desc: The same cue name you played, e.g. "sfx_survival_lp".

nodes.title: Sound: Stop Ambience Loop
nodes.desc: Silence a looping ambience bed. Use the exact stream name you started it with, or it keeps playing.
nodes.desc_short: Silence a looping ambience bed.

params.name: sStreamName
params.desc: The same stream name you started, e.g. "emt_distant_battle_01".

nodes.title: Sound: Unduck Category
nodes.desc: Fades a group back up after a duck, undoing exactly ONE of them. That is the thing to watch: it pops a single level off the stack, so it has to be called once for every Sound: Duck Category you fired. If the count has got away from you, Sound: Clear Ducking wipes the whole stack in one go.
nodes.desc_short: Fades a group back up after a duck, undoing exactly ONE of them.

params.name: sCategory
params.desc: The same mixer group you ducked: "sfx", "music", "ambience" or "vo".

params.name: nFade
params.desc: Seconds to fade back up over. Leave it empty for half a second; 0 snaps back instantly.

returns.name: bOk
returns.desc: True if the request was accepted. It does NOT tell you the group is back to normal - if two ducks were stacked, one unduck still leaves it quiet.

nodes.title: Sound: Master Volume
nodes.desc: Set the game's master volume, optionally fading to it over a few seconds -- handy for ducking everything before a scripted line and bringing it back after. Real shipped scripts only ever use 0 (silent) and 1 (normal); values in between are not confirmed to work.
nodes.desc_short: Set the game's master volume, optionally fading to it over a few seconds -- handy for ducking everything...

params.name: nLevel
params.desc: 0 for silence, 1 for normal volume.

params.name: nFadeTime
params.desc: Seconds to fade over. 0 (the default) snaps to it instantly.

nodes.title: Squad: Dismount And Secure
nodes.desc: Gets a group out of whatever vehicles they are riding and sets them up defending a spot once they are out. Passengers are ejected by the vehicle itself, but a driver has to be pulled out explicitly - confirmed live that the game leaves the driver sitting there otherwise - and this does that for you. Two seconds later, once everyone is really on the ground, the whole group is given a defend order around your point: they hold that area and fight anything that comes inside it. Units already on foot just take the defend order.
nodes.desc_short: Gets a group out of whatever vehicles they are riding and sets them up defending a spot once they are out.

params.name: targetGroup
params.desc: Who dismounts: a team name from Create Team, or a raw list of follower handles.

params.name: atPos
params.desc: The spot to hold, as {x, y, z}. The default is wherever you are standing when this runs.

params.name: radius
params.desc: How big the defended area is, in world units. Bigger lets them chase further from the point before coming back to it.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the dismount and defend went out. False if the group is empty or you gave no position.

nodes.title: Squad: Mount Up
nodes.desc: Loads a whole group into one vehicle in the right order: anyone tagged "driver" with Assign Role climbs in first and takes the wheel before a passenger can claim that seat, then everybody else boards as passengers. It watches until every unit is genuinely seated and then fires the "onVehicleMounted" event; if the vehicle fills up or the way in is blocked it gives up quietly after the timeout, which is a normal outcome here, not an error. Confirmed live: the driver stays commandable through their OWN character handle afterwards - order that follower to move and the vehicle drives there.
nodes.desc_short: Loads a whole group into one vehicle in the right order: anyone tagged "driver" with Assign Role climbs in...

params.name: vehGuid
params.desc: The vehicle to load them into. The default is whatever you are sitting in right now; wire in a spawned vehicle instead if you have one.

params.name: targetGroup
params.desc: Who boards: a team name from Create Team, or a raw list of follower handles.

params.name: opts
params.desc: Optional: { passengerRole = "gunner" to put the non-drivers into turret seats instead of ordinary passenger seats, timeout = <seconds to wait for everyone to be seated, default 20> }.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the boarding orders went out - not a promise everybody fits. False if no vehicle was given or the group is empty.

nodes.title: Squad: Formation Slot Waypoint (debug)
nodes.desc: A live-map diagnostic. While a unit is in formation it is continuously walked toward an invisible marker post that sits at its slot and moves with the leader. This hands you that post, so you can watch a unit's target position travel rather than just watching the unit - the quickest way to see why a formation is not settling into shape. Empty when this unit is not in formation right now.
nodes.desc_short: A live-map diagnostic.

params.name: guid
params.desc: The unit to inspect.

returns.name: anchor
returns.desc: The invisible waypoint object marking this unit's formation slot, or nothing if it is not in a formation.

nodes.title: Squad: Assign Role
nodes.desc: Tags one follower with a job, like "driver" or "heavy". The tag is just a label you pick - nothing about the unit changes by itself. Other nodes read it: Mount Up puts whoever is tagged "driver" into the driver's seat first, before anybody else can claim it, and everyone else boards as passengers.
nodes.desc_short: Tags one follower with a job, like "driver" or "heavy".

params.name: guid
params.desc: The follower to tag.

params.name: roleType
params.desc: Any word you like - "heavy", "medic", "pointman". "driver" is the one with built-in meaning, because Mount Up looks for it.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the tag was stored. False only if no unit was given.

nodes.title: Squad: Cancel Order Sequence
nodes.desc: Stops a running order sequence part-way through and puts the group straight back to following you, which is the safe fallback. Your onCancel code runs if you gave any. A no-op if that group has no sequence running.
nodes.desc_short: Stops a running order sequence part-way through and puts the group straight back to following you, which is...

params.name: targetGroup
params.desc: Whose sequence to stop: the same team name (or the same list of units) you started it with.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if a sequence was running and has now been cancelled. False if there was nothing to cancel.

nodes.title: Squad: Clear Formation
nodes.desc: Stops holding formation. Everybody stays exactly where they are standing - they do NOT go back to following you on their own, because a formation is usually cleared in order to hand the group a different order next. If you want them back at your side, follow this with Order Team set to "follow".
nodes.desc_short: Stops holding formation.

params.name: targetGroup
params.desc: Whose formation to stop: the same team name (or list of units) you set it on.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the group was found and its formation slots were stopped. False if the group is empty.

nodes.title: Squad: Create Team
nodes.desc: Names a group of your followers so you can command them separately - 'alpha' takes the hill while the rest of your roster keeps guarding the truck. Only real followers can be on a team: anyone in the list who is not on your roster is quietly dropped. Calling it again with the same name replaces that team's membership rather than adding to it. The name "__all__" is reserved by the system and refused.
nodes.desc_short: Names a group of your followers so you can command them separately - 'alpha' takes the hill while the rest of...

params.name: teamName
params.desc: What to call this team. You use this same name in every other Squad node.

params.name: guids
params.desc: The members, as a list of follower handles. The default puts your entire roster on the team; for a smaller team build a list like { unitA, unitB }.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the team was defined. False only if you gave no name, or used the reserved name "__all__".

nodes.title: Squad: On Event
nodes.desc: Runs your own code when something happens to a squad. It is the very same event system as the Followers On Event node - Squad shares one bus rather than keeping a second. On top of "onRecruit" / "onDismiss" / "onFollowerDown", squad work fires "onStepComplete" (the units, which step number, which behaviour) each time an order sequence advances, "onQueueComplete" (the units) when a whole sequence finishes, and "onVehicleMounted" (the vehicle, the units) once everybody is seated after Mount Up.
nodes.desc_short: Runs your own code when something happens to a squad.

params.name: eventName
params.desc: Which event to listen for: "onStepComplete", "onQueueComplete", "onVehicleMounted", "onRecruit", "onDismiss" or "onFollowerDown".

params.name: fn
params.default: function(guids) Ess.Log("squad event for " .. tostring(#guids) .. " units") end
params.desc: Your code, run each time that event fires. It receives whatever that event sends - see the event list above for what each one passes.

returns.name: stop
returns.desc: Call this to stop listening.

nodes.title: Squad: Order Team
nodes.desc: Gives one command to a single team and leaves the REST of your roster completely alone - your other followers carry on doing exactly what they were already doing. Two teams can be running different orders at the same time without clearing each other's destination markers or yanking each other back to following.
