Same 11 behaviours and same options as Order Everyone, and the same hand-back: an attack ends when its target dies, a move or one-shot patrol ends on arrival, and only that team then returns to following you. An empty or unknown team is a safe no-op.
nodes.desc_short: Gives one command to a single team and leaves the REST of your roster completely alone - your other followers...

params.name: teamName
params.desc: Which team to command, by the name you gave Create Team.

params.name: behavior
params.desc: Which order to give: "follow", "move", "face", "hold", "defend", "attack", "patrol", "flee", "enter", "deploy" or "animate".

params.name: opts
params.desc: The details for that order: { at = {x,y,z} for move/face/defend, points = { {x,y,z}, ... } for patrol, loop = false for a one-shot patrol, target = <enemy handle> for attack or <vehicle handle> for enter, radius for defend, role = "driver" / "passenger" / "gunner" for enter, action for animate, speed, priority }.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the order went out. False if that team currently has nobody alive on it.

nodes.title: Squad: Run Order Sequence
nodes.desc: Runs a list of orders one after another, waiting for each one to actually finish before starting the next: board the truck, drive to the drop point, get out and defend. Unlike a single order, the group does NOT peel off back to following you between steps. A step is finished when a move or one-shot patrol arrives, when an attack's target dies, or when an "enter" step has every unit seated in some vehicle. Anything else (hold, defend, guard, a looping patrol) has no natural finish, so that step simply runs until its time is up and the queue moves on. Every step gets a timeout regardless - 30 seconds unless you set one - so a single stuck unit or blocked path can never freeze the sequence forever. Starting a new sequence for the same group replaces the one already running.
nodes.desc_short: Runs a list of orders one after another, waiting for each one to actually finish before starting the next:...

params.name: targetGroup
params.desc: Who runs the sequence: a team name from Create Team. A raw list of follower handles also works here if you would rather not name a team.

params.name: steps
params.default: { { behavior = "move", opts = { at = { Ess.Object.pos(Ess.Player.character(0)) } }, timeout = 30 }, { behavior = "hold", timeout = 10 } }
params.desc: The steps, in order. Each one is { behavior = <an order name>, opts = { <that order's details> }, timeout = <seconds before giving up on this step, default 30> }. The example walks the group to where you are standing, then has them stand their ground for 10 seconds.

params.name: queueOpts
params.desc: Optional: { onComplete = function() ... end, onCancel = function() ... end } - your own code for when the whole sequence finishes, or when it gets cancelled.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the sequence started. False if you gave no steps, or the group has nobody in it.

nodes.title: Squad: Role Of Unit
nodes.desc: Reads back the job tag you gave a unit with Assign Role. Handy for branching your script on who is the driver, or for showing roles in your own UI.
nodes.desc_short: Reads back the job tag you gave a unit with Assign Role.

params.name: guid
params.desc: The unit to look up.

returns.name: roleType
returns.desc: The role string you assigned, or nothing if this unit was never given one.

nodes.title: Squad: Set Formation
nodes.desc: Makes a group walk in a shape around a leader and keep holding it as the leader moves - each unit is steered to its own slot, recomputed twice a second. This is visual flavour rather than precision tactics, and it looks great behind you. Being in formation takes the units off ordinary following, so anything else that was steering them is stopped first to stop the two fighting over the same unit. They hold the shape until you clear it or give them a different order.
nodes.desc_short: Makes a group walk in a shape around a leader and keep holding it as the leader moves - each unit is steered...

params.name: targetGroup
params.desc: Who forms up: a team name from Create Team, or a raw list of follower handles.

params.name: formationType
params.desc: "wedge" (a V opening forward, the default), "column" (single file directly behind the leader), "line" (a flat wall just behind them) or "diamond" (a ring all the way around the leader).

params.name: opts
params.desc: Optional: { leader = <who they form up on, defaults to you>, spacing = <how far apart the slots sit, default 3> }.

returns.name: ok
returns.desc: True if the formation started. False if the group is empty, or no leader could be found.

nodes.title: Squad: Team Members
nodes.desc: Hands you a team's members as they stand right now. It is checked live every time you read it, so anyone killed or dismissed since you built the team is filtered out - this can never give you a unit that is no longer yours. An unknown team name gives an empty list rather than an error.
nodes.desc_short: Hands you a team's members as they stand right now.

params.name: teamName
params.desc: The team to read, by the name you gave Create Team.

returns.name: guids
returns.desc: The team's currently-alive members, in the order you listed them. Empty if the team is unknown or everyone on it is gone.

nodes.title: Squad: Team Of Unit
nodes.desc: Tells you which team a unit was last put on. This is a convenience lookup, not the authority: somebody who has since been dismissed still shows their old team name here. When you need the truth about who is currently on a team, read Team Members instead.
nodes.desc_short: Tells you which team a unit was last put on.

params.name: guid
params.desc: The unit to look up.

returns.name: teamName
returns.desc: The team name they were last assigned to, or nothing if they were never put on one.

nodes.title: Squad: All Team Names
nodes.desc: Lists every team name you have created, sorted alphabetically so the order is stable. Use it to discover what teams exist. It does not check whether a team still has anybody alive on it, so pair it with the Team Members node when that matters.
nodes.desc_short: Lists every team name you have created, sorted alphabetically so the order is stable.

returns.name: names
returns.desc: A list of team name strings, sorted A to Z. Empty if you have not created any teams.

nodes.title: Remembered Values
nodes.desc: Gives you a table that survives your script being run again. A mod script re-runs from the top on every keypress and every level reload, so ordinary variables reset every single time - anything you put in this table does not. It also merges your defaults field by field, so adding a new default later still takes effect on a table that already exists. The obvious one-line version of this quietly drops newly added fields, which is the real bug this exists to fix.
nodes.desc_short: Gives you a table that survives your script being run again.

params.name: name
params.desc: A name for your mod's storage. Pick one and keep using it - the same name always gives you back the same table.

params.name: defaults
params.desc: The starting fields, e.g. { score = 0, on = false }. Only fields that are missing get filled in, so values you already changed are never overwritten.

returns.name: state
returns.desc: Your table. Read and write fields on it (state.score = state.score + 1) and they are still there next run.

nodes.title: Text: Capitalize
nodes.desc: Upper-cases the very first letter and leaves everything else exactly as it was - for turning a raw word into the start of a sentence.
nodes.desc_short: Upper-cases the very first letter and leaves everything else exactly as it was - for turning a raw word into...

params.name: s
params.desc: The text to capitalize.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The text with its first letter in upper case.

nodes.title: Text: Contains
nodes.desc: Is this shorter piece of text found anywhere inside the longer one? The search is plain literal text, NOT a Lua pattern - so a "." really does mean a full stop, which is the mistake people usually make with Lua's own string.find.
nodes.desc_short: Is this shorter piece of text found anywhere inside the longer one?

params.name: s
params.desc: The text to search inside.

params.name: needle
params.desc: The bit you're looking for.

returns.name: yes
returns.desc: True if it's in there somewhere.

nodes.title: Text: Count Occurrences
nodes.desc: How many times a piece of text shows up inside another. Counted as plain literal text (not a Lua pattern), and overlaps don't double-count. Looking for an empty piece of text gives 0.
nodes.desc_short: How many times a piece of text shows up inside another.

params.name: s
params.desc: The text to search inside.

params.name: needle
params.desc: The bit to count.

returns.name: count
returns.desc: How many times it appears.

nodes.title: Text: Ends With
nodes.desc: Does this text finish with that piece of text? Useful for checking file extensions or name suffixes. Matched as plain literal text, not as a Lua pattern. An empty suffix always counts as a match.
nodes.desc_short: Does this text finish with that piece of text?

params.name: s
params.desc: The text to check.

params.name: suffix
params.desc: The ending you're looking for.

returns.name: yes
returns.desc: True if the text ends with that suffix.

nodes.title: Text: Join
nodes.desc: Glues a list of pieces back into one line of text with a separator between them - the opposite of Text: Split. Handy for turning a list of names into something you can print.
nodes.desc_short: Glues a list of pieces back into one line of text with a separator between them - the opposite of Text: Split.

params.name: list
params.desc: The list of pieces to glue together.

params.name: sep
params.desc: What to put between pieces. Empty glues them with nothing between; ", " gives a readable list.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The joined-up text.

nodes.title: Text: Split Into Lines
nodes.desc: Breaks a block of text into a list of lines, one entry per line. A stray carriage return before a newline is dropped, so text written on Windows works too, and a single trailing newline won't add a phantom empty line at the end.
nodes.desc_short: Breaks a block of text into a list of lines, one entry per line.

params.name: s
params.desc: The block of text to break up.

returns.name: lines
returns.desc: A numbered list of lines, in order.

nodes.title: Text: Pad Left
nodes.desc: Adds padding to the LEFT of some text until it reaches a given width, so numbers line up in a right-aligned HUD column. Pass "0" as the padding character to zero-pad a number. Text that's already long enough comes back untouched.
nodes.desc_short: Adds padding to the LEFT of some text until it reaches a given width, so numbers line up in a right-aligned...

params.name: s
params.desc: The text to pad.

params.name: width
params.desc: How many characters wide the result should be.

params.name: ch
params.desc: The character to pad with. Only the first character is used.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The padded text.

nodes.title: Text: Pad Right
nodes.desc: Adds padding to the RIGHT of some text until it reaches a given width, so labels line up in a left-aligned column. Text that's already long enough comes back untouched.
nodes.desc_short: Adds padding to the RIGHT of some text until it reaches a given width, so labels line up in a left-aligned...

params.name: s
params.desc: The text to pad.

params.name: width
params.desc: How many characters wide the result should be.

params.name: ch
params.desc: The character to pad with. Only the first character is used.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The padded text.

nodes.title: Text: Split
nodes.desc: Chops text into a list of pieces at every separator - the way to read a comma-separated config line or a name like "squad_alpha_2". The separator is plain literal text, not a Lua pattern: this is the classic trap, because splitting on "." with Lua's own tools splits on EVERY character instead. An empty separator gives you one entry per character, and a separator that never appears just gives the whole text as a single piece.
nodes.desc_short: Chops text into a list of pieces at every separator - the way to read a comma-separated config line or a name...

params.name: s
params.desc: The text to chop up.

params.name: sep
params.desc: What to split on. Leave as "," for a comma list; "" splits into single characters.

returns.name: pieces
returns.desc: A numbered list of the pieces, in order.

nodes.title: Text: Starts With
nodes.desc: Does this text begin with that piece of text? Great for spotting names by prefix, like every object whose name starts with "M2_". Matched as plain literal text, not as a Lua pattern.
nodes.desc_short: Does this text begin with that piece of text?

params.name: s
params.desc: The text to check.

params.name: prefix
params.desc: The beginning you're looking for.

returns.name: yes
returns.desc: True if the text starts with that prefix.

nodes.title: Text: Title Case
nodes.desc: Capitalizes The First Letter Of Every Word - for turning an internal name into a readable label on screen.
nodes.desc_short: Capitalizes The First Letter Of Every Word - for turning an internal name into a readable label on screen.

params.name: s
params.desc: The text to convert.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The text with every word capitalized.

nodes.title: Text: Trim
nodes.desc: Strips spaces, tabs and stray newlines off both ends of some text - tidy up a line someone typed before you compare it to anything.
nodes.desc_short: Strips spaces, tabs and stray newlines off both ends of some text - tidy up a line someone typed before you...

params.name: s
params.desc: The text to tidy up.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The text with the outside whitespace removed.

nodes.title: Text: Truncate
nodes.desc: Clips text down to a maximum length and tacks "..." on the end if anything was cut off - so an over-long mission or player name can't blow out your HUD panel. Text already short enough is returned unchanged.
nodes.desc_short: Clips text down to a maximum length and tacks "..." on the end if anything was cut off - so an over-long...

params.name: s
params.desc: The text to clip.

params.name: n
params.desc: The most characters allowed, including the ... .

params.name: ellipsis
params.desc: What to stick on the end when text was cut off.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The clipped text.

nodes.title: Support: Airstrike Flyby
nodes.desc: Sends a support aircraft screaming in over the spot on a single pass, coming in from one side and carrying on past. The pass itself is what you are staging - what the aircraft shoots on the way through is down to the vehicle template, and this node has no owner setting, so kills from it are not credited to a faction. For guaranteed explosions on the ground, fire the Artillery node at the same point alongside it, which is exactly what the game's own one-tap airstrike does.
nodes.desc_short: Sends a support aircraft screaming in over the spot on a single pass, coming in from one side and carrying on...

params.name: x
params.desc: East/west world coordinate the aircraft passes over.

params.name: y
params.desc: Ground height at the spot. The altitude option is measured up from this, so getting it badly wrong can fly the aircraft underground or absurdly high.

params.name: z
params.desc: North/south world coordinate the aircraft passes over.

params.name: opts
params.desc: vehicle = which aircraft makes the pass ('Support Vehicle (Autogunship)'). altitude = height above the spot (120) - drop it for a low, loud pass. speed = how fast it travels (55).

nodes.title: Support: Artillery Barrage
nodes.desc: Rains a barrage of shells over an area - the workhorse 'punish this position' call-in. The rounds land scattered around the point a fraction of a second apart rather than all at once, so it walks in the way a real barrage does and gives anyone in the area a moment to react.
nodes.desc_short: Rains a barrage of shells over an area - the workhorse 'punish this position' call-in.

params.name: x
params.desc: East/west world coordinate of the centre of the barrage.

params.name: y
params.desc: Ground height at the centre. Shells are spawned high above this.

params.name: z
params.desc: North/south world coordinate of the centre.

params.name: opts
params.desc: count = how many shells (5). radius = how far from the centre they scatter (14) - widen it to threaten an area, tighten it to flatten one building. stagger = seconds between each shell (0.35). ammo and owner are passed down to every shell, so 'Artillery Shell' plus owner = 'China' gives China the credit for the whole barrage.

nodes.title: Support: Bombing Run
nodes.desc: A plane runs in and walks a stick of bombs across the target. The bombs are released from wherever the plane actually is at the moment each one drops, a fraction of a second apart, so they land in a LINE along its flight path rather than all on the one point - aim the run at the near end of what you want flattened, not the middle.
nodes.desc_short: A plane runs in and walks a stick of bombs across the target.

params.name: x
params.desc: East/west world coordinate the plane runs in on.

params.name: y
params.desc: Ground height at the target. The altitude option is measured up from this.

params.name: z
params.desc: North/south world coordinate the plane runs in on.

params.name: opts
params.desc: vehicle = the plane ('Support Vehicle (A10)'). ammo = what it drops ('Bomb'). count = how many bombs in the stick (3) - more makes a longer line, not a bigger crater. altitude = height above the target (150). speed = how fast it flies (160), which also stretches or tightens the spacing of the line. owner = a faction NAME so the kills are credited to them.

nodes.title: Support: Gunship Flight
nodes.desc: Sends a flight of attack helicopters over the area, fanned out and arriving one after another rather than in a single clump - the set-piece 'they called in air support' moment. Like the airstrike node this stages the flyby; what the helicopters engage on the way through is the template's own behaviour.
nodes.desc_short: Sends a flight of attack helicopters over the area, fanned out and arriving one after another rather than in...

params.name: x
params.desc: East/west world coordinate the flight passes over.

params.name: y
params.desc: Ground height at the spot. The altitude option is measured up from this.

params.name: z
params.desc: North/south world coordinate the flight passes over.

params.name: opts
params.desc: template = which helicopter to fly ('AH1Z'). count = how many (3). stagger = seconds between each one arriving (1.6). spread = how far apart they fan out (45). altitude = height above the spot (55, much lower than the jet nodes). speed = how fast they travel (45).

nodes.title: Support: Reinforcements
nodes.desc: Brings a squad of units in to a spot, either dropped from a helicopter, parachuted in behind a plane pass, or simply appearing on the ground. They arrive as ordinary spawned units and will do nothing in particular on their own - follow this with an AI Orders: Command node to give them something to do, and file them with Set Group first if you want to command them as one.
nodes.desc_short: Brings a squad of units in to a spot, either dropped from a helicopter, parachuted in behind a plane pass, or...

params.name: x
params.desc: East/west world coordinate where they arrive. They are spaced out in rows around this point so they do not land on top of each other.

params.name: y
params.desc: Ground height where they arrive. Too low buries them, so use a real ground reading rather than a guess.

params.name: z
params.desc: North/south world coordinate where they arrive.

params.name: opts
params.desc: units = the list of templates to bring in; leave it out or empty and NOBODY arrives, though a paradrop plane still flies over, which is the confusing part. Confirmed real infantry templates include 'Allied Soldier', 'Allied Officer', 'Allied Heavy (Light MG)', 'Allied Heavy (AA)' and 'Allied Boss'. deliver = 'copter' for a helicopter drop, 'paradrop' for a plane pass with the units appearing a second or two later, or leave it out entirely and they simply appear on the ground. faction = who the delivery helicopter belongs to ('Allied', 'China', 'Guerilla', 'OC', 'Pirate', 'VZ'), used by the copter delivery only. A blank template name is caught for you because it would otherwise crash the game outright, but the names still have to be ones this level actually knows.

nodes.title: Support: Single Shell
nodes.desc: Drops one artillery shell onto a spot - the single round every other call-in node here is built from. It appears high above the point and falls with an impact fuse, so expect about a second between calling it and the explosion. Nothing to clean up afterwards: the round is a one-shot the engine disposes of itself.
nodes.desc_short: Drops one artillery shell onto a spot - the single round every other call-in node here is built from.

params.name: x
params.desc: East/west world coordinate of the target spot. Normally wired in from a position node rather than typed.

params.name: y
params.desc: Ground height at the target spot. The shell is spawned well above this and falls onto it.

params.name: z
params.desc: North/south world coordinate of the target spot.

params.name: opts
params.desc: ammo = which round to drop; confirmed real ones are 'Gunship Shell', 'Artillery Shell', 'Bomb', 'Cluster Bomb Projectile' and 'Cruise Missile Projectile'. dropHeight = how far above the point it starts (220) - lower it for a shorter delay before impact. owner = a faction NAME such as 'China' or 'Allied' so the game credits the damage and kills to them; leave it out and nobody is blamed for it.

nodes.title: Sys: Build Flags
nodes.desc: Reads what KIND of copy of the game this is - a demo, the censored German release, a shipping build versus a developer one, whether a player profile is loaded at all, and whether the auto-load-last-save path is armed. Branch on these rather than assuming them: the game's own shipped scripts check them defensively because they genuinely vary between builds, and anything a build does not provide reads as false here instead of crashing.
nodes.desc_short: Reads what KIND of copy of the game this is - a demo, the censored German release, a shipping build versus a...

returns.name: build
returns.desc: A bundle of true/false flags: 'demo' (this is demo mode), 'german' (the censored German release, which has different gore and content rules - worth knowing if your mod adds violent content), 'finalConfig' (a released build rather than a developer one), 'hasProfile' (a player profile is loaded, so save-related work makes sense), and 'autoLoad' (the game is set to auto-load the last save).

nodes.title: Sys: Is Loading
nodes.desc: Yes/no: is the engine still loading, or streaming the world in around the player, right now? Check this before you spawn anything - dropping objects into a world that is still assembling itself is a classic source of things that vanish or land in the wrong place. The game's own shipped scripts pair this with 'does the player have a character yet' as their complete 'the world is not ready' test, and copying that pairing is the safe habit.
nodes.desc_short: Yes/no: is the engine still loading, or streaming the world in around the player, right now?

returns.name: bLoading
returns.desc: True while loading or streaming. Always a plain true/false - it never comes back as nothing, so it is safe to branch on directly.

nodes.title: Sys: Language
nodes.desc: Reads the language the player has the game set to, as plain text like 'English'. Any mod that puts words on screen should branch on this, so your custom text matches the rest of the game instead of showing up in English in the middle of a French playthrough.
nodes.desc_short: Reads the language the player has the game set to, as plain text like 'English'.

returns.name: s
returns.desc: The language name, e.g. 'English'. Nil if the game could not be asked.

nodes.title: Sys: Level Name
nodes.desc: Tells you which map is loaded and which master script is running it - in freeplay both come back as 'vz'. Worth checking before a mod does anything, so you are not spawning things into a menu. The trap: at the bare title screen these can be EMPTY TEXT rather than nothing at all, so a 'is a level loaded yet' test has to compare against an empty string, not just check for missing.
nodes.desc_short: Tells you which map is loaded and which master script is running it - in freeplay both come back as 'vz'.

returns.name: sLevel
returns.desc: The name of the loaded map, 'vz' in freeplay. Can be empty text at the title screen.

returns.name: sMasterScript
returns.desc: The name of the game script driving that map, also 'vz' in freeplay. Same empty-text caveat.

nodes.promoted_from_getter: multi-value return cannot be spliced inline as an expression

nodes.title: Sys: Platform
nodes.desc: Tells you which platform the game thinks it is running on, as the engine's own raw number - 3 on a PC build. It is deliberately NOT translated into a friendly name like 'PC', because 3 is the only value anyone has ever actually observed and inventing labels for the rest would be pure guesswork. Compare it against a number you have measured yourself rather than assuming a meaning.
nodes.desc_short: Tells you which platform the game thinks it is running on, as the engine's own raw number - 3 on a PC build.

returns.name: n
returns.desc: The platform number. 3 on this PC build; no other value has been confirmed, so treat anything else as unknown.

nodes.title: Sys: Player Settings
nodes.desc: Reads the player's own option-menu choices in one go, instead of six separate calls. Respect what you find here: a mod that shows spoken dialogue while the player has subtitles turned ON is a bug, and so is drawing HUD-anchored UI while the player has the HUD hidden. Anything the game refuses to answer comes back as false rather than erroring.
nodes.desc_short: Reads the player's own option-menu choices in one go, instead of six separate calls.

returns.name: settings
returns.desc: A bundle of true/false settings: 'subtitles' (show text for spoken lines - match it), 'tutorials' (tutorial prompts wanted), 'rumble' (controller vibration allowed, so check before you shake the pad), 'invertY' (up/down look is flipped), 'confirmOnCircle' (the confirm and cancel buttons are swapped, which changes how you should word a prompt), and 'noHud' (the HUD is hidden, so do not draw anything pinned to it).

nodes.title: Sys: Uptime
nodes.desc: How many seconds the game has been running, measured on the game's own clock - a session that had been up a while read 1354.7. Unlike real-world time this does NOT tick while the game is paused or loading, which makes it the honest answer to 'how long has this person actually been playing' and a good base for anything you want to happen after so much playtime.
nodes.desc_short: How many seconds the game has been running, measured on the game's own clock - a session that had been up a...

returns.name: n
returns.desc: Seconds of game time since the game was launched. Counts from launch, not from when your mod loaded, so record a starting value if you want elapsed time.

nodes.title: Sys: Game Version
nodes.desc: Reads which build of the game you are running - handy for stamping a log line, or for refusing to run a mod on a build you have not tested. Note it hands back TWO separate values, a build code and a data version; taking only the first is the common misread. Both read '100000' on the build this was measured against.
nodes.desc_short: Reads which build of the game you are running - handy for stamping a log line, or for refusing to run a mod...

returns.name: sCode
returns.desc: The build code of the game executable, as text rather than a number.

returns.name: sData
returns.desc: The version of the game's data files, which can in principle differ from the code version above.

nodes.promoted_from_getter: multi-value return cannot be spliced inline as an expression

nodes.title: Table: Compact
nodes.desc: Rebuilds a list so its numbered entries run 1, 2, 3 with no gaps. Fixes a real, nasty bug: setting an entry to nil to "remove" it leaves a HOLE, and Lua's # length is undefined on a holed list, which silently drops or duplicates entries later on. This CHANGES the list you give it. In new code prefer table.remove, which never leaves a hole; this is for cleaning up one that already happened. Named keys are left alone.
nodes.desc_short: Rebuilds a list so its numbered entries run 1, 2, 3 with no gaps.

params.name: t
params.desc: The list with gaps in it.

returns.name: t
returns.desc: The same table, now packed densely from 1 upward.

nodes.title: Table: Contains Value
nodes.desc: Is this value anywhere in the table? Checks every entry, numbered and named alike. Values are compared exactly, so two separate tables with the same contents do NOT count as equal.
nodes.desc_short: Is this value anywhere in the table?

params.name: t
params.desc: The table to search.

params.name: val
params.desc: The value to look for. Written as Lua, so put quotes around text; or wire in a value from another node.

returns.name: found
returns.desc: True if the value is in the table.

nodes.title: Table: Copy
nodes.desc: Makes a separate copy of a table so that editing one doesn't quietly change the other. It's a SHALLOW copy: any tables sitting inside are still shared between the two, not cloned.
nodes.desc_short: Makes a separate copy of a table so that editing one doesn't quietly change the other.

params.name: t
params.desc: The table to copy.

returns.name: copy
returns.desc: A new table with the same entries.

nodes.title: Table: Count
nodes.desc: How many entries a table holds in total, named keys included. Use this rather than Lua's # length, which only ever sees the numbered part and silently ignores named keys.
nodes.desc_short: How many entries a table holds in total, named keys included.

params.name: t
params.desc: The table to count.

returns.name: count
returns.desc: Total number of entries.

nodes.title: Table: Index Of
nodes.desc: The position (1, 2, 3...) of the first entry equal to this value, or nothing if it isn't there. Only looks at the numbered part of the table, so named keys are ignored.
nodes.desc_short: The position (1, 2, 3...) of the first entry equal to this value, or nothing if it isn't there.

params.name: t
params.desc: The list to search.

params.name: val
params.desc: The value to look for. Written as Lua, so put quotes around text; or wire in a value from another node.

returns.name: index
returns.desc: The 1-based position, or nothing if the value isn't in the list.

nodes.title: Table: Is Empty
nodes.desc: True if the table has nothing in it at all - no numbered entries and no named ones either.
nodes.desc_short: True if the table has nothing in it at all - no numbered entries and no named ones either.

params.name: t
params.desc: The table to test.

returns.name: empty
returns.desc: True when the table has no entries.

nodes.title: Table: Keys
nodes.desc: Gives you all of a table's key names as a plain numbered list, so you can walk through them or count them.
nodes.desc_short: Gives you all of a table's key names as a plain numbered list, so you can walk through them or count them.

params.name: t
params.desc: The table to read the keys from.

returns.name: keys
returns.desc: A numbered list of the table's keys (order is not guaranteed).

nodes.title: Table: Merge
nodes.desc: Copies every entry from src onto dst, overwriting where the two clash - the usual way to apply overrides on top of default settings. This CHANGES dst in place and hands it back to you, so pass a copy if you need the original kept.
nodes.desc_short: Copies every entry from src onto dst, overwriting where the two clash - the usual way to apply overrides on...

params.name: dst
params.desc: The table being changed - it receives the entries.

params.name: src
params.desc: The table to copy entries from. Its values win any clash.

returns.name: dst
returns.desc: The same dst table, now with src's entries merged in.

nodes.title: Table: Reverse
nodes.desc: Gives back a new list with the order flipped back to front. The original list is left alone.
nodes.desc_short: Gives back a new list with the order flipped back to front.

params.name: t
params.desc: The list to flip.

returns.name: reversed
returns.desc: A new list in the opposite order.

nodes.title: Table: Slice
nodes.desc: Pulls out a new list containing just entries i through j, counting from 1 and including both ends. Leave the numbers off to take the whole list; numbers past the ends are pulled back in rather than causing an error.
nodes.desc_short: Pulls out a new list containing just entries i through j, counting from 1 and including both ends.

params.name: t
params.desc: The list to take a piece of.

params.name: i
params.desc: First entry to take, counting from 1. Defaults to the start.

params.name: j
params.desc: Last entry to take (included). Defaults to the end.

returns.name: slice
returns.desc: A new list holding just that stretch of entries.

nodes.title: Table: Values
nodes.desc: Gives you all of a table's values as a plain numbered list, throwing the keys away - handy when you only care about the contents.
nodes.desc_short: Gives you all of a table's values as a plain numbered list, throwing the keys away - handy when you only care...

params.name: t
params.desc: The table to read the values from.

returns.name: values
returns.desc: A numbered list of the table's values (order is not guaranteed).

nodes.title: Text Console: Close
nodes.desc: Close the typing console and give the player back control of their character if it was locked. Safe to call even when nothing is open.
nodes.desc_short: Close the typing console and give the player back control of their character if it was locked.

nodes.title: Text Console: Is Open
nodes.desc: Check whether the typing console is currently open and eating keystrokes. Use it to stop your own key handler from reacting to letters the player is trying to type.
nodes.desc_short: Check whether the typing console is currently open and eating keystrokes.

returns.desc: True while the console is open.
returns.name: ok

nodes.title: Text Console: Open
nodes.desc: Open a yellow prompt line at the top-left of the screen for the player to type into -- no .gfx asset needed, just a plain text widget. Unlike UI: Text Prompt this is a REPL: Enter runs your onSubmit and clears the line but leaves the console OPEN, and only Escape closes it. By default it freezes the player's movement and actions while typing; set lockPlayer = false for a chat box that leaves the game running underneath.
nodes.desc_short: Open a yellow prompt line at the top-left of the screen for the player to type into -- no .gfx asset needed,...

params.name: opts
params.default: { prompt = "SAY: ", max = 200, lockPlayer = true, onSubmit = function(sText) Ess.Hud.banner(sText) end }
params.desc: Settings table: prompt (text before the caret, default "> "), text (what it starts with), max (character limit, default 200), lockPlayer (default true), onSubmit(text), onCancel(), onChange(text).

nodes.title: Time: Clock
nodes.desc:
A self-advancing stopwatch for 'how long since the last tick', which is what you need to make movement or drain rates run at the same speed no matter how often your loop ticks.

Each reading gives the seconds since the PREVIOUS reading and is capped, so a pause or a stutter cannot hand you a huge jump that flings something across the map.
nodes.desc_short: A self-advancing stopwatch for 'how long since the last tick', which is what you need to make movement or...

params.name: maxDelta
params.desc: The cap, in seconds. Any longer gap - a pause, a loading hitch - is reported as this instead of the real time. Leaving it empty means 0.25.

returns.name: clock
returns.desc: The clock. Reading it is a method, so there is no node for it - type clock:delta() into a Lua field inside your loop's action. Each call resets the measurement, so read it ONCE per tick and reuse the number.

nodes.title: Time: Cooldown
nodes.desc:
Builds a reusable 'am I allowed to do this again yet' checker, so you do not hand-roll a stamp, a comparison and a reset every time.

The FIRST check is always allowed - a freshly made cooldown is ready immediately, not blocked as though it had just been used. Asking while it is still cooling returns no and does NOT push the window back, so hammering the key cannot keep it locked forever.

Keep the checker somewhere that survives your script re-running, or every key press builds a brand new one that is ready again.
nodes.desc_short: Builds a reusable 'am I allowed to do this again yet' checker, so you do not hand-roll a stamp, a comparison...

params.name: seconds
params.desc: How long the lockout lasts. Leaving it empty means one second.

returns.name: ready
returns.desc: The checker. Call it in a Lua field - ready() gives true and immediately starts the next window, or false if you must wait. Store it in an Ess.State table; a new one from a re-run is always ready again.

nodes.title: Time: Elapsed
nodes.desc:
How many seconds since that stamp was marked.

Reading it does NOT advance or reset anything, so it is safe to check on every tick and always get the true answer - only Time: Re-Mark moves the start. That is what makes 'has ten seconds passed yet' reliable here.
nodes.desc_short: How many seconds since that stamp was marked.

params.name: uStamp
params.desc: The stamp to measure from, wired in from a Time: Mark Now node.

returns.name: seconds
returns.desc: Seconds since the mark, as a decimal. Comes back as 0 if the stamp is missing - so a timer that reads 0 forever usually means nothing is wired in.

nodes.title: Time: Format
nodes.desc: Turns a raw number of seconds into a tidy display string, so a HUD stopwatch or countdown does not read as 87.43219. Feed it a Time: Elapsed value.
nodes.desc_short: Turns a raw number of seconds into a tidy display string, so a HUD stopwatch or countdown does not read as...

params.name: nSeconds
params.desc: The number of seconds to format, usually wired from Time: Elapsed.

params.name: bUseTenths
params.desc: Show tenths of a second as well - worth it for a tense countdown, distracting on a long timer.

returns.name: text
returns.desc: The display string. Comes back empty if the engine's formatter is unavailable, so do not assume you always have text.

nodes.title: Time: Mark Now (Game Clock)
nodes.desc:
The same as Time: Mark Now, but on the GAME clock: it freezes while the game is paused and slows down with Time: Set Scale.

Pick this one for gameplay cooldowns that should stop counting while the player is in a menu, and the real-world one for UI timing that should not.
nodes.desc_short: The same as Time: Mark Now, but on the GAME clock: it freezes while the game is paused and slows down with...

returns.name: stamp
returns.desc: An opaque handle to feed to Time: Elapsed or Time: Re-Mark.

nodes.title: Time: Re-Mark
nodes.desc: Resets a stamp you already have back to now - restarting that stopwatch without making a new one. This is how a repeating cooldown works: check elapsed, act, re-mark.
nodes.desc_short: Resets a stamp you already have back to now - restarting that stopwatch without making a new one.

params.name: uStamp
params.desc: The stamp to reset, wired in from a Time: Mark Now node. Empty does nothing.

nodes.title: Time: Restore Scale
nodes.desc: Puts the world back to normal speed - the same as setting the scale to 1, under the name you will actually look for. Every slow-motion effect needs one of these, and it is worth running once at the start of a script too, in case a previous run died before it could clean up.
nodes.desc_short: Puts the world back to normal speed - the same as setting the scale to 1, under the name you will actually...

nodes.title: Time: Set Scale
nodes.desc:
Changes how fast the game world runs - slow motion for an explosion or a finishing move.

IT STAYS. This is a global setting with no timer on it: set 0.2 and the whole game is five times slower until something sets it back. Always pair it with Time: Restore Scale, and be careful in a script that can crash halfway through and leave the player stuck in slow motion.
nodes.desc_short: Changes how fast the game world runs - slow motion for an explosion or a finishing move.

params.name: n
params.desc: Speed multiplier: 1 is normal, 0.2 is five times slower, above 1 is faster. Very small values make the game feel frozen.

nodes.title: Time: Since
nodes.desc: Exactly the same as Time: Elapsed, under a name that reads better in some graphs ('since I started this'). Same behaviour, same numbers - pick whichever makes your graph clearer.
nodes.desc_short: Exactly the same as Time: Elapsed, under a name that reads better in some graphs ('since I started this').

params.name: uStamp
params.desc: The stamp to measure from.

returns.name: seconds
returns.desc: Seconds since the mark, or 0 if the stamp is missing.

nodes.title: Time: Mark Now (Real Clock)
nodes.desc:
Marks this instant and hands you a stamp to measure from later - the start of a stopwatch. Ask Time: Elapsed how long it has been.

This is the REAL-WORLD clock: it keeps counting through pauses, menus and slow-motion. Use it for UI, cooldowns on your own tools, and anything that should not freeze with the game.

Remember the stamp somewhere that survives - in a script that re-runs on every key press, a plain local is gone by the next press, so put it in an Ess.State table.
nodes.desc_short: Marks this instant and hands you a stamp to measure from later - the start of a stopwatch.

returns.name: stamp
returns.desc: An opaque handle, not a number - you cannot subtract it or print it, only feed it to Time: Elapsed or Time: Re-Mark.

nodes.title: Track: Track Custom Cleanup
nodes.desc:
The escape hatch: register any cleanup of your own to be run when the tracker closes, for something Ess has no dedicated node for - resetting a variable, restoring time scale, putting a setting back.

Wire in the SAME tracker the rest of your feature registers into, or this lands in a fresh bin that never gets closed.
nodes.desc_short: The escape hatch: register any cleanup of your own to be run when the tracker closes, for something Ess has...

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.Track to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: closeFn
params.desc: A no-argument action to run at teardown. Anything that is not actually a function is silently ignored - it is handed straight back to you but never registered, so nothing will run.

returns.name: closeFn
returns.desc: The same function back, unchanged, so it can be chained onward.

nodes.title: Track: Track Anything
nodes.desc:
The one to reach for. Hand it ANY of the things Ess gives you to turn something off and it will be torn down with the rest when the tracker closes - a stop from an On: node, a marker handle, a loop's name, or an object that knows how to cancel itself.

That is the whole point: you no longer have to remember which namespace spells cleanup which way. The typed nodes below are still better when you know exactly what you are holding, but this is the one that always works.

Wire in the SAME tracker every node registers into. The default builds a fresh empty one right here, which is valid Lua but puts this in a bin nobody will ever close.
nodes.desc_short: The one to reach for.

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.Track to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: x
params.desc: The thing to tear down later, wired in from whatever made it. A loop's name must be typed WITH quotes ('MyMod.tick') - without them it reads as a variable and tracks nothing. Anything empty is quietly ignored.

returns.name: x
returns.desc: The same thing back, unchanged, so you can carry on using it in the very next node instead of splitting into two steps.

nodes.title: Track: Close Everything
nodes.desc:
The payoff. Ends everything this tracker collected, in one action - every hook released, every spawned object removed, every marker cleared.

It works backwards, newest first, because things you made later usually depend on things you made earlier and tearing down in that order is what avoids surprises. Afterwards the tracker empties itself: safe to call twice, and safe to keep using, since anything registered later starts a fresh batch.

This MUST be the same tracker the things were registered into. The default builds a brand new empty one, which cheerfully succeeds and tears down absolutely nothing - if your cleanup 'does not work', check that first.
nodes.desc_short: The payoff. Ends everything this tracker collected, in one action - every hook released, every spawned object...

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.Track to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

nodes.title: Track: Add Context Action And Track
nodes.desc:
The third that DOES as well as tracks: it attaches a context action - the on-screen 'press this to use it' prompt on an object - and registers its removal for teardown, so the prompt cannot linger on an object after your feature is gone.

Like the disposer, removal uses the SAME object handle you passed in, not a separate one.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.
nodes.desc_short: The third that DOES as well as tracks: it attaches a context action - the on-screen 'press this to use it'...

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.Track to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The object to put the prompt on, wired in. Empty registers nothing.

params.name: sLabelOrKey
params.desc: The label shown to the player, or a localisation key.

Any further arguments the engine's context-action call wants, typed as raw Lua and separated by commas. Real examples vary a lot - anywhere from none to half a dozen - so only the object and label above are a fixed shape. Leave empty if you are unsure.

returns.name: uGuid
returns.desc: The same object handle back, so it can be chained onward.

nodes.title: Track: Add To Disposer And Track
nodes.desc:
Another that DOES as well as tracks: it hands an object to the engine's disposer under a category now, and registers the matching removal for teardown.

Worth knowing: unlike a hook or a marker, the removal here takes the SAME object handle you passed in rather than some separate handle the engine gives back - so there is nothing extra to hold on to.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.
nodes.desc_short: Another that DOES as well as tracks: it hands an object to the engine's disposer under a category now, and...

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.Track to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The object to add, wired in. Empty registers nothing.

params.name: sCategory
params.desc: The disposer category to file it under - a plain piece of text you choose.

returns.name: uGuid
returns.desc: The same object handle back, so it can be chained onward.

nodes.title: Track: Track Event Hook
nodes.desc:
Registers an engine hook you ALREADY created so it gets deleted at teardown. Hooks are never cleaned up for you, and a hook left behind keeps firing into a feature that no longer exists.

Shortcut: the Event: Hook Engine Event node has its own tracker input that does exactly this in one step - use that instead unless you are tracking a hook made some other way.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.
nodes.desc_short: Registers an engine hook you ALREADY created so it gets deleted at teardown.

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.Track to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The handle the hook handed back when it was created. An empty one is quietly ignored, which means nothing gets cleaned up.

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: The same handle back, so you can keep using it to unhook early if you want to.

nodes.title: Track: Track Spawned Object
nodes.desc:
Registers something you SPAWNED so it is removed from the world at teardown - the fix for a test script that leaves a field of abandoned vehicles behind after a dozen runs.

CAREFUL: this DELETES the object when the tracker closes. Only ever track things your own mod created. Tracking the player's car, or an NPC that belongs to a mission, means your cleanup destroys it.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.
nodes.desc_short: Registers something you SPAWNED so it is removed from the world at teardown - the fix for a test script that...

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.Track to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The handle of the object you spawned, wired in from the node that spawned it. Left empty this registers nothing at all - which is safer than the alternative, so it is deliberately not filled in for you.

returns.name: uGuid
returns.desc: The same object handle back, so you can spawn, track and use it in one chain.

nodes.title: Track: Track Raw Marker
nodes.desc:
Registers a RAW engine marker handle so it is removed at teardown.

This is for the low-level marker layer only. A handle from Mark: Object or Mark: Zone is NOT one of these - it is a bundle of several surfaces plus possibly an anchor prop, and it needs Mark: Clear. Put those through Track: Track Anything instead, which routes them correctly. Passing one here fails quietly and your markers stay on screen.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.
nodes.desc_short: Registers a RAW engine marker handle so it is removed at teardown.

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.Track to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: handle
params.desc: A handle from a raw marker call. If it came from a Mark: node, use Track: Track Anything instead.

returns.name: handle
returns.desc: The same handle back, unchanged.

nodes.title: Track: New Tracker
nodes.desc:
One bin for everything a feature creates, so switching the feature off is a single action instead of a checklist you will get wrong.

WHY IT EXISTS: on this engine every Add has a matching Remove and there is no 'remove everything I made' for ANY of them - spawned objects, markers, event hooks, radar and PDA blips all leak if you forget one. A tracker is that missing function.

Its registrars are methods, so they have no nodes of their own - type them into any Lua field: tracker:guid(u) for a spawned object, tracker:marker(h), tracker:event(h), tracker:any(x) for anything at all, then tracker:closeAll() to tear the lot down. You can also wire the tracker straight into the Event: Hook node's tracker input.
nodes.desc_short: One bin for everything a feature creates, so switching the feature off is a single action instead of a...

returns.name: tracker
returns.desc: The bin. tracker:closeAll() runs every teardown in reverse order - newest first, which is the order that does not surprise - then empties itself. Safe to call twice, and safe to keep using afterwards: anything added later is a fresh batch.

nodes.title: Track: Track PDA Blip
nodes.desc:
Registers a PDA map blip you already added so it is removed at teardown. Like the radar one, it is tracked by the NAME you registered it under rather than a handle, and the name has to match exactly or nothing is removed.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.
nodes.desc_short: Registers a PDA map blip you already added so it is removed at teardown.

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.Track to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: sName
params.desc: The exact name the blip was added under - text, not a handle.

returns.name: sName
returns.desc: The same name back, so it can be passed straight on.

nodes.title: Track: Add Quality And Track
nodes.desc:
Different from most of the nodes here: this one DOES the thing as well as tracking it. It applies an engine quality to an object now, and registers the matching removal for teardown, so a temporary property cannot outlive the feature that applied it.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one, or the quality is never taken off again.
nodes.desc_short: Different from most of the nodes here: this one DOES the thing as well as tracking it.

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.Track to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: uGuid
params.desc: The object to apply the quality to, wired in. Empty simply fails quietly and registers nothing.

params.name: nQuality
params.desc: The engine's numeric id for the quality. These are engine constants, so look the right number up rather than guessing - a wrong one fails silently rather than erroring.

returns.name: ref
returns.desc: The reference the engine handed back, or nothing if it did not take. Nothing coming back means the quality was never applied, so check that before wondering why the effect is missing.

nodes.title: Track: Track Radar Objective
nodes.desc:
Registers a radar objective you already added so it is removed at teardown. Unlike most things here you track it by the NAME you registered it under, not by a handle - that is what the engine's remove call wants.

The name must match exactly or the teardown silently removes nothing and the blip stays on the radar for the rest of the session.

Wire in the shared tracker, not a fresh one.
nodes.desc_short: Registers a radar objective you already added so it is removed at teardown.

params.name: instance
params.desc: The Ess.Track to call this on. The default builds a fresh one inline, which works but makes a new one every call -- wire in a shared one if you need the same instance across nodes.

params.name: sName
params.desc: The exact name the objective was added under. This is text, not a handle, and a typo here is a leak you will not notice until the blips pile up.

returns.name: sName
returns.desc: The same name back, so it can be passed straight on.

nodes.title: Triggers: Arm
nodes.desc: Waits for something to happen in the world and then runs your code - the player walking into an area, a target dying, a building dropping below half health, an area being cleared out, or simply a timer. This is what turns a static set of spawns into an encounter that reacts. Most conditions work by quietly checking a few times a second and will keep checking forever until they fire, so hand it a tracker or hold on to the cancel handle.
nodes.desc_short: Waits for something to happen in the world and then runs your code - the player walking into an area, a...

params.name: spec
params.desc: What to wait for. Leave blank to fire immediately. {once = 5} fires once after 5 seconds. {recurring = 10, limit = 3, delay = 2} fires every 10 seconds, at most 3 times, starting after 2. {proximity = 25, at = {x,y,z}} fires when the player gets within 25 of that spot. {onDestroy = 'SomePlacementName'} fires when that named thing in the level dies - if the name is not found it is logged and this never fires. {onDestroy = {at = {x,y,z}, radius = 45, kind = ...}} finds the nearest matching object in the area and then watches THAT one die, re-checking every second until something is actually there, which is how you arm on a target that has not spawned yet. {onHealthBelow = {target = <handle>, pct = 50}} fires at half health, measured against the health it had when you armed this, not its maximum - arm it on an already-damaged target and the bar you are measuring from is that damaged value. {onCleared = {at = {x,y,z}, radius = 45, kind = ..., faction = ...}} fires when a populated area becomes empty, and it has to SEE something there first, so arming it over an already-empty patch waits forever.

params.name: onFire
params.desc: Your code, run once the condition is met. A recurring trigger runs it again on every tick.

params.name: tracker
params.desc: Optional but strongly recommended. Hand it an Ess.Track and every timer this schedules gets cleaned up with the rest of your setup, instead of a poll quietly running for the rest of the session.

returns.name: cancel
returns.desc: A stop handle. Keep it and feed it to an Ess.stop node to disarm the trigger, even if its condition is met later. Without it (and without a tracker) a waiting trigger cannot be called off.

nodes.title: UI: Progress Bar
nodes.desc: Show a labelled progress bar on screen -- fuel, health, a capture meter, a download timer. It appears immediately at whatever starting value you give it, and you move it afterwards with handle:set(0.75) or relabel it with handle:label("AMMO"). Values below 0 or above 1 are clamped. TRAP: needs the ui_bar.gfx movie deployed with your mod or nothing shows.
nodes.desc_short: Show a labelled progress bar on screen -- fuel, health, a capture meter, a download timer.

params.name: opts
params.desc: Settings table: x, y (position, default 20/330), w, h (size, default 300x36), label (text beside the bar), value (0 to 1).

returns.desc: The bar widget handle -- call :set(0..1), :label(s), :show(), :hide() on it.
returns.name: result

nodes.title: UI: Contract Board
nodes.desc: Open a big two-pane board: a scrolling list of 12 rows down the left, and a details pane on the right holding a category line, up to 4 reward lines, up to 8 objective lines, plus a progress bar and progress text. This is what the game-style contract-selection screen is built from. Fill the right-hand pane with handle:detail{...}; onSelect fires every single time the cursor moves, which is where you refresh it. TRAP: needs the contracts.gfx movie deployed with your mod, and needs focus = true to respond to keys.
nodes.desc_short: Open a big two-pane board: a scrolling list of 12 rows down the left, and a details pane on the right holding...

params.name: opts
params.default: { x = 60, y = 60, title = "CONTRACTS", hint = "UP/DOWN MOVE   ENTER ACCEPT   LEFT BACK", focus = true, items = { { header = "AVAILABLE" }, { label = "Oil Field Raid" }, { label = "Convoy Ambush" } }, detail = { category = "OIL FIELD", rewards = { "$5000", "Fuel +200" }, objectives = { "Destroy 3 tanks", "Reach the LZ" }, progress = 0.4, progressText = "2/5" } }
params.desc: Settings table: x, y (default 60/60), w, h (default 660x420), title, hint, items (same row shape as UI: Scrolling List), empty, detail (the right pane: category, rewards, objectives, progress 0..1, progressText), focus = true to give it the keyboard, onSelect(item, i, board), onChoose(item, i, board), onBack(board).

returns.desc: The board widget handle -- call :items(t), :detail(t), :select(i), :selected(), :title(s), :hint(s), :show(), :hide(), :focus() on it.
returns.name: result

nodes.title: UI: Chat Log
nodes.desc: Show a scrolling message log with 5 visible lines and an optional typing line underneath -- a chat window, or a running feed of what's happening. Add lines with handle:push("text") (long lines wrap at 52 characters) and start typing with handle:prompt(). Set autoHide to a number of seconds and the window fades out that long after the last message and pops back on the next one; it deliberately never fades while you are typing in it. Leave autoHide out and it stays on screen permanently. TRAP: needs the chat.gfx movie deployed with your mod.
nodes.desc_short: Show a scrolling message log with 5 visible lines and an optional typing line underneath -- a chat window, or...

params.name: opts
params.default: { x = 20, y = 400, title = "COMMS", autoHide = 8, onSubmit = function(sText) Ess.Hud.radio(sText) end }
params.desc: Settings table: x, y (default 20/400), w, h (default 360x132), title, max (lines kept in the buffer, default 60), autoHide (seconds -- omit to stay visible forever), onSubmit(text) for what the player types.

returns.desc: The chat widget handle -- call :push(s), :prompt(), :title(s), :clear(), :show(), :hide(), :focus() on it.
returns.name: result

nodes.title: UI: Yes/No Dialog
nodes.desc: Pop a modal yes/no box in the middle of the screen and grab the keyboard: Left/Right switch between the two buttons, Enter picks, Escape counts as no. It deliberately starts with NO highlighted, so a stray Enter never confirms something destructive. Your onResult then runs with true or false and whatever had the keyboard before gets it straight back. Only one dialog exists at a time -- opening a second one reuses and overwrites the first. TRAP: needs the ui_confirm.gfx movie deployed with your mod.

nodes.title: UI Theme: Apply Changes
nodes.desc: Pushes the whole theme into the UI and redraws whatever is already on screen - this is what makes a restyle actually appear while the game is running. You only need it when widgets already exist: if you set your colours before the first widget is ever created, that widget picks them up on its own and this is unnecessary. It pushes every setting rather than only the changed ones, deliberately, so the UI can never end up half-way between two themes. Safe to call when no UI exists at all, and safe to call before the UI movie has finished loading.

nodes.title: UI Theme: Read Setting
nodes.desc: Reads what a theme setting is actually worth right now - your override if you set one, otherwise the stock default. Always read values this way rather than looking at Ess.UI.Theme.something directly: a setting nobody has touched is genuinely empty on the theme table, with the real value living behind it in the defaults, so reading the table straight gives you nothing for most keys. It is also the intended way to pull the shared palette into your own code - "warn" and "danger" are drawn by nothing at all and exist purely so your mod's own colours follow whatever theme is active.

Sizes and spacings come back as plain numbers in CANVAS units, not pixels: "rowHeight", "titleHeight", "padding", "radius", "sizeTitle", "sizeBody", "sizeSmall". "panelAlpha" is 0-100 opacity and "font" is text. A name that isn't a real setting comes back empty rather than erroring.

A name that isn't one of the built-in ones leaves the theme completely untouched and writes a line to the log saying so, because a mistyped preset name would otherwise just look like theming being broken.

nodes.title: UI: Anchor To An Edge
nodes.desc: Works out the concrete x, y, width and height for a box you want pinned to an edge of the screen, so you never have to do that arithmetic yourself. The whole point is that "8 in from the right" gets resolved against the canvas width as it really is right now; if you instead write x = 640 - 160 - 8 by hand you have quietly baked in a 4:3 assumption. That precise mistake is why toasts used to appear about 213 units left of the true edge on every widescreen display. Use this for anything anchored right, bottom, or centred.

If you give both left and right, right wins; same for top and bottom. Leave the whole thing out and you get a 100 x 24 box in the top-left corner.

nodes.title: UI: Canvas Width
nodes.desc: Reads how many units wide the UI's drawing area currently is - the number to measure a right-hand edge against. These are CANVAS units: not pixels, and not percentages. The canvas is the movie's fixed 853x480 stage divided by the global scale, so at the default 75% it is 1137 units across and stays 1137 whether the player is on 1080p, 1440p or 4K - there is nothing to work out per-resolution. It does move when the scale changes, though, so read it rather than writing the number down.

nodes.title: UI: Is Widescreen
nodes.desc: Answers whether the game considers the display widescreen. That decides how much room the UI really has: on widescreen its box matches the movie's stage one-for-one at 853 units across, and on 4:3 the same stage is letterboxed into a 640-wide space instead. The catch is that the game only ever reports a CATEGORY, not an actual aspect number, so 16:10 answers yes here and is treated as 16:9 - the same approximation the game makes for itself. If the question cannot be answered at all, this quietly says no rather than erroring.

nodes.title: UI: Screen Size
nodes.desc: Reads the whole drawing area in one go - width, height, and the game's own word for the display shape. The first two are CANVAS units (the 853x480 stage divided by the global scale, so 1137x640 at the default 75%), which means they change when YOU change the scale, not when the player changes resolution. The third is a trap worth knowing: the game answers with a CATEGORY word like "WIDESCREEN", never a number like 1.78, so it is text and you cannot do maths on it. nodes.title: UI: Set Global Scale
nodes.desc: Sets how big the whole UI kit draws, as a percentage. It scales everything together - boxes, chrome and text - because shrinking only the font would leave the words rattling around inside boxes that stayed the same size. The counter-intuitive part: scaling DOWN gives you a BIGGER canvas to lay out in, since the canvas is the movie's fixed 853x480 stage divided by this number - at the default 75 you get 1137x640 units. So a box written at fixed coordinates shrinks as you'd expect, but a box whose size came from the canvas keeps filling the screen and just gets finer text and borders. Takes effect immediately and is safe to call over and over while you tune it.

params.name: pct
params.desc: The scale as a percentage. 75 is the kit's default, picked on a 1440p display by judging real small menu text rather than a demo grid - 45 and 55 were both tried first and read too small. Anything under 25 or over 200 is clamped to those. Leave it blank and you get 100.

returns.name: pct
returns.desc: The scale that was actually used, after clamping to 25-200.

returns.desc: How many canvas units wide the drawing area is now - 1137 at 75%.

returns.desc: How many canvas units tall the drawing area is now - 640 at 75%.

nodes.title: UI: Widget Rectangle
nodes.desc: Reads the size of the single on-screen box that the entire UI kit lives inside, measured in the engine's own widget space - 853x480 on widescreen, or 640x360 letterboxed on 4:3. Note what it deliberately does NOT do: it ignores the global scale entirely. The rectangle's job is to map the movie's stage onto the screen, and the scale's job is to shrink the content inside that stage - apply the scale to both and you count it twice, which is exactly the bug an earlier version had (a 520-unit panel covered 61% of the screen instead of the 27% its numbers implied, so everything looked enormous at 100% and only sane around 10%). You will rarely want this; lay out in canvas units instead.
